#9105. Ultimate Guide to 4A Hair: Care Tips, Styles, and Maintenance

Understanding your hair type is key to achieving healthy, luscious curls. Hair types range from 1 to 4 — straight, wavy, curly, and coily — with type 4 being the curliest. Type 4A hair has a fine texture and loose curl pattern, forming springy coils that need special care to stay healthy and vibrant.

Knowing your hair type helps determine the best hair care routine. Caring for 4A hair is essential, whether you’re dealing with dryness or breakage or want to define your curls.

Let’s dive into the world of 4A hair and discover how to keep those curls popping.

Alright, curl friends, let’s break it down. Hair type falls into four main categories:

Now, Type 4 hair is where things get seriously curly and coily. Within this category, we’ve got subtypes A, B, and C,

which refer to the width and density of your curls.

So, what’s the deal with 4A hair? 4A hair is the queen of the fine, loose curl pattern. It forms tight, springy coils that are like tiny, perfect S-shapes. These curls are less dense than their 4B and 4C cousins, making them more defined and delicate. Think of 4A hair as the Goldilocks of coily hair — not too tight, not too loose, but just right.

Your hair is unique and gorgeous, but it requires a bit of extra TLC to keep it looking its best. Here’s a straightforward guide to keeping your 4A hair moisturized, healthy, and thriving:

4A hair tends to be dry as its coily structure makes it difficult for natural oils to travel down the hair shaft. Keeping it moisturized is essential, so incorporate a good leave-in conditioner into your daily shampooing routine. Use deep conditioning treatments weekly to replenish moisture and strengthen your curls.

Don’t forget scalp care, too! For maximum hydration, look for products with ingredients like shea butter, coconut oil, and glycerin.

4A hair is prone to tangles, so detangle gently to avoid breakage. Use a wide-tooth comb or your fingers to work through knots carefully. Start from the ends and work your way up to the roots, and always detangle when your hair is wet and coated with conditioner to provide slip and minimize damage.

Heat styling tools can cause significant damage to 4A hair, leading to dryness, breakage, and loss of curl pattern. Minimize the use of blow dryers, flat irons, and curling wands. If you use heat, always apply a heat protectant spray first to shield your hair from high temperatures.

Pro tip: To maintain the health of your curls, opt for air-drying or styles that don’t require heat.

Protective styles like braids, twists, and buns can help reduce manipulation and minimize breakage. These styles tuck away your ends, protecting them from friction and environmental damage.

Cotton pillowcases cause friction, which leads to frizz and breakage, especially for 4A hair. Switching to satin or silk pillowcases instead helps mai

ntain your curl pattern and prevent tangles.

Regular trims are crucial for keeping 4A hair healthy and preventing split ends from traveling up the hair shaft. Aim to trim your hair every 8-12 weeks to remove damaged ends and keep your curls looking fresh and vibrant.

Yes, 4A hair is curly and falls under the coily category. It features tight, springy curls that form an S-shape.

To determine your hair type, look at the curl pattern, texture, and density. 4A hair has a loose curl pattern with fine, springy coils, while 4B and 4C hair have tighter curls. 3C hair is curly but not as tight as Type 4.

Washing once a week or every two weeks is generally sufficient for 4A hair. Overwashing can strip the hair of its natural oils.

Regular trims every 8-12 weeks help keep 4A hair healthy by removing split ends and preventing breakage.

Taking care of your 4A hair isn’t rocket science, but it does need a little know-how and the right tools.

Love those natural curls — keep them hydrated, avoid excessive heat, and give them some nighttime TLC.

#9104. Arches create “animated silhouette” at red-brick apartment block in King’s Cross

Two-storey-tall arches frame entrances to Cadence, a mixed-use apartment block in King’s Cross, London, which has been completed by local studio Alison Brooks Architects.

Positioned at the northern end of Lewis Cubitt Park, the prominent red-brick building combines 163 apartments alongside commercial and social spaces organised around an open-air courtyard.

Signposted by its two towers, the building by Alison Brooks Architects forms part of the wider King’s Cross redevelopment and is complete with views overlooking Heatherwick Studios’ Coal Drops Yard to the south.

According to studio founder Alison Brooks, the building’s red-brick exterior was chosen to pay homage to the nearby St Pancras Station, while its arched openings draw on the area’s neo-gothic architecture and were conceived as a “civic welcoming gesture”.

“The main concept of the project was to make a clear statement of welcome and arrival in King’s Cross, but from the north end of the master plan rather than the south end, which everybody is familiar with,” Brooks told Dezeen.

“My first instinct was to respond to King’s Cross’ iconic railway station architecture, sculpting the site massing to create an animated silhouette. A language of two-story high arches creates a really generous, welcoming gesture at street level and toward the park,” she added.

The building is formed of a five-sided block, with no designated front or back, which rises to form two towers reaching 12 and 16 storeys respectively.

For its construction, the studio opted for a Design for Manufacture and Assembly approach, which saw 85 per cent of the building’s components prefabricated off-site.

At the centre of its angular plan, an open-air courtyard, complete with a reflecting pool, has been wrapped by sheltered walkways that provide a shared circulation space between the building’s private and commercial programmes.

“It’s a multifaceted building,” Brooks said. “Each facet of the pentagon has a particular identity or address to the space that it’s adjacent to.”

“This idea of making a very connected space at the base of the building, even though it’s a courtyard, is visually trying to connect all the sides of the plot to the city around it.”

“It’s a place of movement and light and also a kind of special quality because of the reflecting pool,” she added.

The building’s first two floors have been dedicated to 633 square metres of commercial and social spaces, which include a “community living room” that opens onto the courtyard at ground level.

A prefabricated lift system connects to the upper floors, where the 163 residential units benefit from both courtyard and street views.

A combination of rectangular and arched windows draws daylight into the building’s white-walled interior, complemented by private balconies and communal roof terraces.

Other projects developed as part of the King’s Cross regeneration include Google’s landscraper office building by architecture studios BIG and Heatherwick and an office block designed by Coffey Architects to recall the area’s industrial spaces.

#9103. landmark james turrell exhibition to inaugurate superblue kyoto in early 2027

opening opposite teamLab biovortex kyoto, the new venue places one of the most influential explorations of light in contemporary art within a growing cultural district.

Superblue, the Miami-based experiential art company, opens its first international art center in Kyoto, Japan, in early 2027, with a major exhibition dedicated to American artist James Turrell. Located in the Kyoto Station Southeast Area, directly opposite teamLab Biovortex Kyoto, the venue brings together two distinct approaches to immersive art, contributing to a wider initiative to establish the neighborhood as a cultural destination. The inaugural exhibition traces Turrell’s six-decade exploration of light and space, presenting one of his largest solo exhibitions in Japan.

Founded in 2020, Superblue develops and presents large-scale experiential artworks that place visitors within the work. Its first permanent venue opened in Miami in 2021, presenting installations by artists including Es Devlin, teamLab, and Turrell.

Superblue Kyoto occupies the Kyoto Station Southeast Area, a neighborhood included in a City of Kyoto revitalization initiative seeking to establish cultural and creative hubs, with an emphasis on art, culture, and younger generations. Directly across from Superblue stands teamLab Biovortex Kyoto, which opened in October 2025 as the collective’s largest museum in the country. The two buildings share a distinctive indigo-blue exterior and will face one another, creating a concentrated destination for visitors interested in large-scale, immersive art.

For Kyoto, a city whose cultural identity is closely associated with its historical architecture, temples, and traditional arts, the development introduces another layer to its contemporary cultural landscape. The pairing of Superblue and teamLab offers a new point of encounter between international contemporary art, technological experimentation, and the city’s ongoing efforts to develop creative spaces.

Since beginning his artistic practice in the 1960s, Turrell has treated light as the primary material of his work. His installations manipulate color, depth, and spatial perception, often making light appear almost tangible while destabilizing the viewer’s understanding of the surrounding environment. One of his earliest experiments, Afrum-Proto (1966), uses a projection of white light onto the corner formed by two walls. The resulting geometric shape creates the illusion of a solid, three-dimensional cube emerging from the architecture.

Over the following decades, Turrell developed several interconnected bodies of work, including his Projection Pieces (1966–69), Skyspaces (1974–), and Ganzfelds (1976–). Each series approaches perception differently, using controlled light conditions to alter the relationship between the viewer and the artwork. His most ambitious undertaking remains Roden Crater, an extinct volcano in Arizona’s Painted Desert that he has been transforming into a monumental naked-eye observatory since 1977. Its chambers and tunnels frame the sun, moon, stars, and planets, turning natural celestial events into constructed perceptual experiences.

At Superblue Kyoto, a broad selection of works will trace this development from the artist’s early experiments to his more recent installations. Visitors will encounter environments that invite them to reconsider how they perceive color, distance, depth, and space. The exhibition’s individual artworks and complete presentation are expected to be announced in December 2026.

#9102. Pucker Up! How to Heal Cracked Lip Corners Fast

Smiling for selfies should be fun, not painful! If cracked lip corners or angular cheilitis make it hard to smile, eat, or kiss, don’t worry. Check out these tips to heal those cracks quickly. With some care and good habits, you’ll have pain-free, makeout-ready lips in no time. Say goodbye to angular cheilitis and hello to a happier smile!

The first step to healing your cracked lip corners quickly is to lock in any moisture. Reach for a product dermatologists call an occlusive, which creates a protective barrier that prevents your lip corners from getting drier. Vaseline, Aquafor, or CeraVe ointment are common occlusives that will help reduce cracking.

Dab a little coconut oil, olive oil, or fragrance-free moisturizer on the corners of your lips daily after you shower. Make it a daily habit, but don’t go overboard. A little dab will do. Allow your skin’s natural oils to build back up as the cracking fades. Bonus tip: Add the occlusive lip barrier after moisturizing.

Locking in moisture only works if you have enough moisture, so staying hydrated is key! Keep a refillable water bottle with you as your trusty sidekick. Sip on plain water throughout the day, or jazz it up with a splash of cucumber or another non-acidic flavor. Pro tip: Avoid lemon juice, which can irritate and sting sensitive skin.

Bonus: Staying hydrated will help your raw lip corners heal quicker and improve your skin’s overall health.

Have you noticed that moisture is a common theme here? Lend your lips a humid hand by sleeping with a humidifier beside your bed. Adding moisture to the air is especially helpful for your cracked lips during the winter or in hot, dry climates. Think about popping a small humidifier in your workspace or wherever you spend the most time.

It might seem like a quick fix to lick your lips to keep them moist, but that can make things worse. Saliva evaporates quickly, leaving a sticky residue that can attract bacteria and lead to infection. So, keep your tongue away from your lips and remember this: “Licking your lips will cause them to lickety-split.”

Whether from frigid cold or dry heat, your skin can lose water rapidly, causing cracking, flaking, discoloration, or swelling. So avoid jumping from a sweltering afternoon at the beach into a freezing cold movie theater.

Also, skip the hot showers or cold plunges for a bit. These types of rapid temperature changes will quickly dry out your lip corners. Bonus tip: Your lips can take a beating from the sun, so find a lip balm with SPF protection.

If your cracked lip corners don’t improve or become especially painful or swollen in a few days, it’s time to visit a board-certified dermatologist. If left untreated, angular cheilitis can last for years, leaving your lips discolored or scarred.

FYI: Angular cheilitis might not appear as clearly in people with darker skin. Instead of turning red, the affected skin may look pale and have a darker border.

Remember that lickety-split mantra? It’s for real. Saliva can get deposited in the corners of your lips for many reasons, like drooling, smoking, or sleeping with your mouth open due to some sniffles. Bacteria grows in those little saliva pools, triggering an inflammatory response that causes your lip corners to get irritated and crack.

Following these tips will make your lips feel better in about a week. Really bad cases of angular cheilitis can take a few weeks. Avoid smoking and eat a balanced diet to get faster results.

As mentioned above, Vaseline and other occlusives help create a protective barrier over the cracked lip corners, which helps the healing process.

You might have woken up with cracked lip corners, but you won’t be able to get rid of them overnight. Be patient and follow the tips above!

Say goodbye to painful cracked lip corners in about a week with these easy tips:

Talk to a dermatologist for customized care if your lip corners become red, swollen, or more painful after a few days.

#9101. Neri Oxman experiments with fabric pigment created by bacteria

Designer Neri Oxman has created a fabric dyeing concept where a bacterial solution is sprayed onto a 3D-knitted silk textile and left to grow a living culture producing faded indigo and pink pigments.

The project, called Vigils, was developed by the designer’s studio, Oxman, for designers, artists and collaborators to “create new forms of material and aesthetic expression”.

Tussah silk thread within the fabric is coated with “bacterially sensitive chemicals”, which act as “a bioreactor” once mixed with the spray.

The fabric then sits for 24 hours, during which the solution and chemicals begin to interact and eventually produce a living bacterial culture. This organism, “numbering in the billions of cells”, spreads across the fabric and converts amino acids into the pigments Indigo and Melanin.

For the process, the Oxman lab created a spray solution containing the BL21 strain of Escherichia coli (E. coli), a strain commonly used in biotechnology and synthetic biology research, and sprayed it onto a silk fabric.

Its growth pattern is directed by “where and how densely the designer directed the culture to grow” via the spray, according to the team.

The fabric is then washed and dried, removing the bacteria, but the pigment remains.

“The microorganisms respond to signals associated with the textile substrate, making biological activity an active component of the material process,” said the team. “Vigils is a research-driven exploration of biological textile colouration.”

“The project is intended to investigate the interaction between synthetic biology and material systems rather than to represent a fully optimised industrial dyeing process.”

The studio created a series of four capes to demonstrate the technique. They display the variations in the muted colours and patterns created by the bacteria.

The studio is presenting the process as a possible alternative to “resource-intensive” industrial dyeing processes.

“The result is not simply an alternative way of applying color: the biological process becomes part of the design itself, producing patterns and variations that could not be achieved through conventional dyeing and making each textile an expression of the process that created it,” said Oxman.

It has not undergone extensive Life Cycle Assessment, which measures its environmental outputs, and is still in the prototype stage.

Neri Oxman opened a New York studio in Midtown Manhattan in 2024 and unveiled an AI-designed skyscraper to demonstrate its computational abilities at the time.

The designer is known for her work in material ecology, but she also faced allegations of plagiarism in her PhD thesis completed at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology.

#9100. Pratt's evolving courses reflect "broader shift in creative practice"

From architects using digital fabrication tools to how graphic designers can enhance their work with AI, Pratt Institute has responded to the increasing fluidity of creative careers by launching three new flexible programmes.

Pratt Institute’s School of Continuing and Professional Studies (SCPS) offers flexible programmes for both working creatives and lifelong designers who want to develop new skills without putting their careers on hold.

Its three certificate programs – Graphic Design, Fine Art and AI design – reflect how creative practice is rapidly evolving.

Pratt’s Graphic Design course focuses on the fundamentals of professional practice and creative production.

From covering typography and branding to composition and visual systems, students apply these skills across digital, print, motion and interactive media.

Its Fine Art course offers small, interactive groups where students curate a portfolio, complement another area of study or return to an existing creative practice. Interdisciplinary experts teach the course within Pratt’s dedicated art studios.

Pratt students explore artificial intelligence (AI) for research, visualisation, ideation and production within its AI Design course, while also considering questions of authorship, ethics and responsible design.

Here, Pratt treats AI as a creative tool rather than a replacement for creative thinking.

“The emphasis remains on human creativity, with technology extending what designers can explore and produce,” the organisation said on its AI course.

The organisation explained that the launch of its latest courses responds to how career paths are changing.

For example, designers are moving between studios and start-ups, consulting and collaborative research, and need to quickly develop new skills to keep up with technology changes.

“Creative careers are becoming more fluid, and education is changing with them,” said Pratt. “Continuing education at Pratt is no longer only about changing careers. For many creatives, it is a way to stay curious, deepen an existing practice and respond to an industry that is constantly changing.”

Pratt added that its courses also reflect a broader shift in creative practice.

For example, designers are increasingly expected to move between physical and digital environments, combine technical skills with conceptual thinking and quickly adapt as new tools and technologies emerge.

Each course covers these aspects and is designed to build on the skills the individual isn’t as strong in.

It added that designers also benefit from a community experience at Pratt. For example, designers, architects, artists, creative technologists and entrepreneurs learn alongside each other, exchanging ideas and forging professional connections that “extend beyond the classroom”.

Pratt’s courses are available in person at Pratt’s Manhattan and Brooklyn campuses and in hybrid formats, making it possible to fit study around work, everyday life and freelance projects.

For more information about Pratt’s courses, visit its website or contact scps-noncredit[at]pratt.edu.

#9099. What Does Dark Green Poop Mean? Causes, Diet, and When to See a Doctor

Bum nuggets typically sport a classic brown, so glancing back into the loo and spying on greenish-colored poop can throw you for a loop.

Most of the time, green poop reflects a leafy diet or your body’s unique way of breaking things down. But if the green becomes a recurring (fecal) matter, it might be something else.

Continue reading to learn more about poop color, its meaning, and when it’s time to make an appointment with a healthcare provider.

Spotting green or another unexpected color in the toilet can be startling, but it’s more common than you might think. From dietary influences to your body’s digestion speed, several factors can change poop from earthy tones to other shades. Let’s check some out.

Are you chowing down on lots of green leafy veggies like spinach, kale, or broccoli? These foods are high in chlorophyll, which can dye your doodles green. Chlorophyll doesn’t always break down entirely before reaching your intestines, meaning it passes through your system and colors your stool green.

Have you ever had a St. Paddy’s Day-themed milkshake or a brightly colored cake? Artificial colors in foods and drinks can change poop from brown to green. It’s not magic! It’s just the dye in green food passing through your gut unchanged.

When your digestive system processes food too rapidly, it doesn’t allow for the full breakdown of bile, a yellow-green fluid that aids digestion. This often results in a greenish stool, especially during fast-moving episodes of diarrhea.

Have you recently been taking antibiotics? These meds can reset your gut’s bacterial crew. Since these tiny critters play a big part in the shade of your stool, introducing antibiotics might cause green poop sometimes.

If you’ve had certain medical treatments, it can affect digestion and cause bright green poop. One example is graft-versus-host disease, which may occur with bone marrow transplants. This tricky condition can bring about less-than-welcome guests, like diarrhea and green stool. It’s a clear signal from your body that things are out of sync.

Some uninvited microscopic guests like Salmonella bacteria, the water-loving mini parasite Giardia, and norovirus can also be a reason for your poop turning green. These critters can hustle your digestion at an unnaturally quick pace, turning your stool green as they disrupt your gut’s usual rhythm.

Babies can surprise you with a whole crayon box of poop colors, and green is definitely in the mix.

For infants, green stool might stem from the same factors as adults, like dietary changes. This includes adjustments when they start eating solids or changes in a parent’s diet if chestfeeding.

Another harmless cause could be ingesting a small amount of amniotic fluid in the womb. So, if you notice your little one sporting some spring grass-colored diapers, it’s usually no biggie.

If the green theme park in your toilet isn’t closing down, or if it’s accompanied by other symptoms like severe stomach pain, nausea, or diarrhea, it might be time to call in the pros. Persistent changes in stool color may signal underlying health issues that need medical attention.

Dark green poop can result from eating lots of leafy greens or foods with green coloring. However, it can also indicate that food travels quickly through the digestive system.

While liver issues can change stool color, they usually turn it pale or dark, not green. If you’re worried about liver health, look for pale or clay-colored stools instead.

If you haven’t been on a kale-eating spree, dark green poop might be from iron supplements or constipation remedies, which can also give poop a greenish tint.

Dark poop could be a sign of your diet or medications. However, if it’s black and tar-like, it might mean bleeding in your upper gastrointestinal tract. In that case, chatting with a healthcare professional is a must.

While green poop can def throw you through a loop, it’s usually not a sign of anything serious. It’s often your body’s way of dealing with what you eat or how fast you digest. So, unless it’s paired with other worrying symptoms, there’s probably no need to panic.

#9098. meet the wienermobile, the 1930s quirky pedal car that put hot dogs on wheels

from its first appearance on american roads in 1936 to its miniature interpretations by bird corporation and konek, the oversized hot dog has become an enduring piece of advertising and automotive culture.

First introduced in 1936, the Oscar Mayer Wienermobile began as a traveling advertisement shaped like an oversized hot dog. Over the decades, the vehicle has gone through several redesigns, but its distinctive silhouette has remained central to the identity of the brand, turning an unconventional marketing idea into a familiar sight on American roads. Its recognizable form has also inspired toys, merchandise, and unusual experiences. In 2019, Oscar Mayer even transformed a full-size Wienermobile into a one-night Airbnb stay in Chicago, inviting guests to eat, live, and sleep inside the eight-meter-long vehicle (find designboom’s previous coverage here).

Now, two vintage Oscar Mayer Wienermobile pedal cars, produced by Bird Corporation and Konek Inc., are appearing together at auction on Bring a Trailer. Offered as a single lot without a reserve, the two new-old-stock examples are described as having never been ridden by children.

The story of the Wienermobile begins in 1936, when Carl G. Mayer, nephew of Oscar Mayer founder Oscar F. Mayer, proposed a hot dog-shaped vehicle as a traveling advertisement for the company’s products. Built by Chicago’s General Body Company, the original measured approximately four meters long and featured a metal body shaped like an oversized wiener, mounted on wheels. Its two open cockpits accommodated a driver and Little Oscar, the promotional character of the brand.

As the vehicle became an established part of Oscar Mayer’s advertising, successive generations introduced new interpretations of the original concept. The 1958 model, designed by industrial designer Brooks Stevens, introduced a rounded, bubble-like front and more integrated bun-shaped elements. Later versions experimented with larger bodies, updated chassis, and elaborate interiors, always retaining the unmistakable hot dog silhouette.

Oscar Mayer discontinued the program in the late 1970s, shifting its attention toward television advertising. Public enthusiasm for the vehicle, however, prompted its return in 1986 for the company’s 50th anniversary. New generations followed, and the Wienermobile resumed its travels across the United States, appearing at parades, public gatherings, supermarkets, and promotional events.

Over the years, the hot dog on wheels inspired toys, merchandise, and other branded interpretations, translating its instantly recognizable shape into objects that could be collected and played with. The two pedal cars now offered at auction on Bring a Trailer belong to this broader history.

Although they share the same orange-and-yellow color scheme, the Bird Corporation and Konek examples feature different construction methods. The Bird version has a single-piece, hot-dog-shaped plastic body mounted over a yellow base, while the Konek model uses a two-piece orange body with Oscar Mayer and Wienermobile decals across its front, rear, and sides.

Both combine molded plastic exteriors with metal frames, orange wheels, yellow seats, and black steering wheels with yellow horn buttons. Twin foot pedals power the miniature vehicles, while faux headlights, grilles, taillights, and windows complete their automotive appearance. The Konek example measures approximately 114 centimeters long, 53 centimeters wide, and 48 centimeters tall.

Today, the Wienermobile remains part of Oscar Mayer’s identity, with six vehicles operated by parent company Kraft Heinz. Its continued presence on American roads speaks to the unusual longevity of a marketing idea conceived in the 1930s. The hot dog-shaped vehicle has become a recognizable piece of American visual culture and continues to inspire new interpretations nearly 90 years after its first appearance.

The two pedal cars’ appearance at auction offers a chance to revisit the history of the Wienermobile, a promotional vehicle that brought advertising, automotive design, and popular culture together. First introduced in 1936, the hot dog-shaped vehicle has evolved into an enduring fixture of American popular culture.

#9097. Batek Architekten designs Berlin orthodontic clinic that looks more like a boutique or gallery

Avoiding the sterile appearance of most medical interiors, Berlin-based Batek Architekten used soothing shades of pastel yellow and matt silver to bring a sense of softness to orthodontic clinic Hey.

Described by its designers as “quietly playful”, Hey combines its two-tone palette with bold geometric elements.

These include a folded steel reception counter, a sculptural bench, and a criss-cross coat rail.

Treatment rooms feature translucent walls of glass-fibre-reinforced plastic, while lighting tubes trace graphic lines across the ceiling.

The result is a space that could be mistaken for a high-end fashion boutique or an art gallery.

“We decided early on to work almost monochromatically,” said studio founder Patrick Batek.

“A soft pastel yellow runs from the floor up across the walls, enveloping visitors and creating a warm, comforting atmosphere.”

Batek Architekten‘s scheme, overseen by Batek and architect Julia Jensen, evolved from a brief set by the client, doctor Julie Charlotte Angrick, who wanted a clinic where young patients would feel comfortable.

It was this that led Angrick to name it Hey, intended as an informal welcome.

“Most visitors are children and teenagers, and many of them come regularly over several years,” explained Batek.

“We wanted to create a place that takes away the fear of the clinical environment without being childish,” he told Dezeen.

“Instead of colourful decoration, we chose radical reduction.”

The same thinking shaped the visual identity developed by graphic design studio Bailey und Bailey, which includes a logo incorporating a smiley face emoticon.

The visual aesthetic didn’t come at the expense of functionality or hygiene.

Located in the north of Berlin, the 178-square-metre clinic occupies a former pharmacy. The architects completely cleared and reconfigured the floor plan, optimising the flow of patients through different spaces.

Textiled tiles line wet rooms and other surfaces that are likely to be touched often, while the yellow-toned floor was cast from a plant-based resin. This floor was the biggest challenge of the project.

“A surface like this needs a perfect substrate, because every irregularity underneath would become visible,” said Batek.

“Preparing the subfloor required great precision, but it was essential for the continuous yellow to work as one uninterrupted surface.”

The architects completed the design by picking out a few elements in red, matching the sign on the wall of the reception area.

These include room numbers, chairs and signs indicating toothbrushing areas.

Cabinets are integrated into the walls, allowing tools and equipment to be hidden away.

“The space is reduced but never cold,” added Batek. “Above all, it reflects the personality of the client and her way of working with young patients.”

The studio has previously also revamped the T7.2 dental clinic in Berlin and renovated a historic cinema in the same city.

#9095. Spring Allergies Can Cause Headaches. Here’s How to Deal

A stuffy nose and itchy, watery eyes are spring-allergy cornerstones—but they’re not the only symptoms that herald a pollen influx for some people. You might not immediately suspect a pulsing headache is due to allergies, but experts say it’s a common occurrence.

In fact, the same immune response that fills your nose with snot or leaves you sneezing up a storm can make your head throb. That’s especially true “if you have multiple seasonal allergies, for instance to grass and tree pollen; live near farms; or spend a lot of time outside during allergy season, being bombarded by pollen,” Beth Oller, MD, a family medicine physician in Stockton, Kansas, tells SELF. Keep reading to learn why allergies can spark headaches, plus how to tell if your head pain is allergy-related and find relief.

If you have spring allergies and breathe in pollen, “your immune system perceives it as a foreign invader,” Dr. Oller says, and releases a bunch of inflammatory chemicals like histamine. The resulting inflammation triggers swelling in your nasal cavities, which are connected to your sinuses, Rekha Raveendran, MD, allergist and immunologist at The Ohio State University Wexner Medical Center, tells SELF. The sinuses extend behind the cheekbones, eyes, and bridge of the nose, and up into the forehead—so when they get puffy, you can wind up with a sensation of facial pressure and also headache, she explains.

At the same time, experiencing the effects of spring allergies may spark migraine attacks in those with migraine. The surge of inflammation and congestion can irritate a nearby nerve that plays a role in migraine, and allergy-driven fatigue and insomnia can be migraine triggers in and of themselves. Research suggests that among people with migraine, those who also have allergies tend to have worse, more frequent attacks than those who don’t.

An allergy headache typically feels like a dull throbbing in your temples, cheeks, or forehead, and makes your face feel heavy. It comes along with congestion, Dr. Oller says, and lying down or tilting your head can increase the pressure. (FYI: This is the same kind of pain as you’d get with a sinus headache, which is caused by a viral or bacterial infection in your sinuses—both lead to mucus buildup and swelling within the sinuses.)

By contrast, migraine attacks (whether or not they’re precipitated by allergies) trigger intense pain on one side of the head. They often come along with nausea, and sensitivity to light and sound, which you would not typically find with allergy headaches, Dr. Raveendran says. Meanwhile, tension headaches tend to feel more like a band squeezing around the head, and cluster headaches spark a surge of pain in or around one eye.

If you get walloped with allergy headaches each year, Dr. Oller suggests starting on an oral antihistamine medication right about now. Pollen counts are rising, and antihistamines take a week or two of daily use to kick in, she explains. The non-drowsy options work best for daytime—think: cetirizine (Zyrtec), levocetirizine (Xyzal), loratadine (Claritin), or fexofenadine (Allegra). You can use the sleepiness-inducing diphenhydramine (Benadryl) at night, but just know that you shouldn’t make a habit of relying on it as a sleep aid.

Both doctors suggest pairing oral allergy meds with a nasal corticosteroid spray like fluticasone (Flonase) or triamcinolone (Nasocort). “They hit those mucus membranes and help decrease inflammation in that region,” Dr. Oller says. It’s best to take both drugs daily throughout allergy season, she adds, not just when you think you need them. (If your headaches are barely alleviated, or the pollen counts in your area are sky-high, you may also be able to safely increase your dose of these allergy meds to boost their efficacy.)

The less pollen that enters your airspace, the fewer symptoms you’ll experience. But you don’t have to stay cooped up to cut your exposure. Keeping your windows closed, using a high-efficiency particulate air (HEPA) filter in your HVAC system (or a portable air purifier that has one), and vacuuming often can make a difference, according to Dr. Oller.

Whenever you do spend ample time outside, Dr. Oller says to rinse off once you get home. This way, you’re not inhaling pollen any longer than you have to. While you’re at it, “shower your sinuses too,” Dr. Oller adds, with a nasal saline spray or Neti Pot. This helps clear some mucus to release pressure and offer temporary relief, Dr. Raveendran says.

If the congestion is making it feel like your face is chock-full of mucus, you might be tempted to reach for an OTC oral decongestant. But take note: While pseudoephedrine (Sudafed) can be helpful, it’s not recommended to use it more than a few days in a row, and isn’t a good choice if you have high blood pressure, Dr. Raveendran says. It’s a stimulant that can make some people feel jittery, or cause a fast heart rate or insomnia.

Nasal decongestants, which include phenylephrine- or oxymetazoline-based sprays (like Afrin and Vicks Sinex), can open up your nose fast but should only be used for three days at a time max, Dr. Raveendran adds. “There’s a risk of rebound congestion that leads to overall worsening of symptoms and addiction to the nasal decongestants,” she says.

Sometimes you just need in-the-moment relief for the head pain. In that case, you can pop an OTC pain reliever like ibuprofen (Advil), naproxen (Aleve), or acetaminophen (Tylenol), Dr. Oller says. The former two may be better at resolving allergy headaches because they combat inflammation. But it’s not advised to take these non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs for more than 10 days straight (unless your doctor tells you otherwise) because of potential effects on your stomach and kidneys. Tylenol, by contrast, is generally safer to take long-term, though shouldn’t be combined with alcohol due to the risk for liver damage.

If you find that your allergy headaches have you reaching for pain relievers more than a few days in a row, check in with your primary care doctor or allergist. They may recommend a more intensive treatment, like prescription steroids, or suggest seeing an ear, nose, and throat doctor or neurologist, in case something else might be behind your head pain.

#9094. John Tree forms sculptural Hoop lamp from pine for Vaarni

Designer John Tree has created the monolithic Hoop Table Lamp for Finnish brand Vaarni, combining an “almost brutalistic block of solid pine” with a hooped shade of thin pine veneer.

Vaarni, which is known for its pine furniture and accessories, used Finnish pine from a sustainably managed forest for the lamp.

Tree‘s design for the light, which was made locally in Jurva, Finland, combines two different pieces of pine to create a sculptural shape.

“One is this heavy, almost brutalistic block of solid pine that forms a stable structural element through which a single cut is made to support the second element – a hoop of thin veneer which forms a diffuser and allows light to come through in an almost magical way,” he told Dezeen.

The hoop has an integrated light source to create a diffused glow, with Tree basing the thickness of the pine used on its ability to let the light through.

The designer also let the materials lead the way when it came to the size of the shade.

“It was in some ways an exercise in reducing the two elements to their simplest geometric forms, yet governed very much by what material would allow,” he said.

“For example, we discovered that if the thin veneer hoop became any bigger, it started to distort under its own weight,” he continued.

“Thickening it was not an option, as this stopped light from going through so we naturally arrived at an optimum form defined by the material.”

While Tree has worked with pine before, he said he hasn’t previously had the opportunity to explore the material’s properties to the extent he did for this project.

“The expertise that Vaarnii have with this material meant that we could do some very precise and complex technical details,” Tree said.

“It was interesting to see how much a material can be elevated with care and precision in its manufacture,” he continued.

“Hoop is a little celebration of pine, a humble material that can do some amazing things.”

Vaarni has previously showcased “brutal and sophisticated” furniture at 3 Days of Design and designed a chair and footstool with Faye Toogood.

#9093. making room for nature: the urban landscapes of kongjian yu

turenscape’s ecological landscapes show how wetlands, waterways, and restored habitats can become part of urban infrastructure, making room for both people and other forms of life.

In Landscapes for Adaptation: Evidence from China, architect and Harvard professor Charles Waldheim examines 60 built experiments realized by Chinese landscape architect Kongjian Yu and his practice Turenscape over the past two decades.

Analyzing their environmental performance, the book documents how landscape architecture can respond to flooding, climate volatility, and ecological change through implemented projects. These built experiments offer a starting point for exploring a broader question: can cities be designed as shared habitats for humans and other forms of life?

Yu, founder of Turenscape and a leading advocate of the sponge city concept, has spent decades arguing that urban development should work with natural processes. His approach uses landscape as infrastructure, allowing water, vegetation, and existing ecological systems to play an active role in addressing flooding, pollution, and habitat loss.

In Shanghai, Houtan Park demonstrates how landscape architecture can make ecological processes part of the urban fabric. Designed by Turenscape and completed in 2010 for the Shanghai World Expo, the 14-hectare park occupies a former industrial site along the Huangpu River. Once used by a steel factory and shipyard, the land was heavily degraded, while the adjacent river was severely polluted. The design builds on the industrial past of the site, transforming its existing landscape into a new ecological and public space. A constructed wetland runs through the park, using a sequence of terraces, cascades, and wetland plants to treat polluted river water.

The system was designed to treat approximately 2,400 cubic meters of water per day, improving its quality from Lower Grade V to Grade III for non-potable uses. The wetland also forms part of the flood-management strategy of the park, while its planted river edge creates conditions for aquatic and bird habitats. Reclaimed industrial materials, agricultural terraces, and a network of paths connect these ecological functions with the public experience of the park.

Water treatment, flood protection, habitat creation, and public access operate within the same landscape. Houtan Park makes infrastructure visible, allowing visitors to encounter environmental processes that are usually hidden behind concrete walls and underground networks.

A related approach appears in Yichang Yunhe Park in Hubei province. Designed by Turenscape and completed in 2013, the 12-hectare project transforms twelve polluted, abandoned fish ponds into what the practice describes as a ‘green sponge’. The design uses the existing water bodies as the foundation for a system that cleanses polluted canal water and remediates contaminated stormwater.

The project relies on regenerative design and minimal intervention. The former ponds become part of a wider landscape of vegetation and water, while paths and elevated walkways allow people to move through the site. Its significance lies partly in the decision to work with an existing, damaged landscape.

In Ningbo, the Yinzhou Central River Transformation explores the potential of restoring an urban waterway. Completed in 2010, the project introduces wetland planting along the riverbanks, alongside walkways and areas for public use. The intervention softens the engineered edges of the river, retaining its role as part of the city’s water infrastructure.

These are some examples of Turenscape’s projects that suggest that ecological urbanism does not necessarily depend on introducing untouched nature into the city, but it can also involve reconsidering infrastructure that already exists: drainage channels, abandoned ponds, industrial waterfronts, and flood-control systems. Such sites become opportunities to restore ecological functions, changing how people encounter water and landscape. However, creating landscapes that manage water and support vegetation is not necessarily the same as designing cities around the needs of other forms of life.

In Yu’s projects, wetlands and planted riverbanks help reduce flooding, improve water quality, and provide habitats. Their value also depends on whether other species can thrive there, how ecological systems develop over time, and how well these landscapes are maintained. In her 2016 book Staying with the Trouble: Making Kin in the Chthulucene, feminist theorist Donna Haraway challenges the idea that humans exist separately from the rest of the living world, describing life as a network of interdependencies in which organisms and environments shape one another. Her concept of sympoiesis, or making-with, offers a way to understand the world as something produced collectively rather than controlled by a single species.

Seen through Haraway’s ideas, Yu’s projects can be understood as more than infrastructure for managing water and flooding. The wetlands and river corridors also create environments where plants, insects, birds, microorganisms, and aquatic species interact. This shifts the focus from what these landscapes provide for people to the wider ecological relationships they support and how these relationships shape urban life.

This does not mean that ecological infrastructure automatically produces a more-than-human city. A landscape can support biodiversity while remaining primarily designed around human priorities. Its ecological value depends on factors such as long-term maintenance, water quality, habitat connectivity, and whether different species can establish and survive. The presence of vegetation or the appearance of a natural landscape is not, on its own, evidence of a functioning ecosystem.

There are also social questions to consider. Green infrastructure can improve urban environments, but it does not necessarily address unequal access to public space, the displacement of existing communities, or the uneven distribution of environmental benefits.

Ecological restoration can become part of wider redevelopment processes, sometimes increasing land values and changing who can afford to live nearby. Assessing these projects therefore requires looking beyond their environmental performance to consider how they affect both local communities and other forms of life.

The projects documented in Waldheim’s Landscapes for Adaptation: Evidence from China demonstrate how landscape architecture can contribute to climate adaptation through built, functioning systems. Their significance extends beyond the technical integration of water management and public space. They suggest that cities can be understood as environments shaped by relationships between human activity and ecological processes.

Yu’s work offers a practical foundation for this shift, while Haraway’s thinking invites us to take its implications further. If cities are understood as shared environments, their success cannot be judged solely by how efficiently they protect people from environmental change. It must also be considered in terms of the relationships they allow to develop between different forms of life. The more-than-human city is not necessarily a finished ecological utopia, but an ongoing process of learning how to live alongside the many species and systems that already make urban life possible.

#9092. How to Calculate Your Rising and Moon Sign: A Beginner’s Guide

The sun sign is the *it girlie* of the “big three” elements in astrology.

But do you know about your moon sign and rising sign?

We chatted with an astrologer to understand what they are and how to calculate them.

According to Olga Verkhotina — astrologer and personal coach — the big three in astrology are your three most significant chart elements:

“While a natal chart contains so many more intricate details beyond just three elements, the big three is a way to determine the main highlights that make up your personality and overall temperament,” Verkhotina says.

Verkhotina explains that a rising sign is the zodiac sign that falls at the beginning of your First House — basically, the beginning of your natal chart.

“The First House in astrology is associated with a person’s identity, individual activity, even their appearance, and the sign that houses that theme gives its characteristics,” she says.

“Knowing your rising sign describes the way others may perceive you, the way your behavior comes across, as well as how you approach new situations in life.”

You’ll need: date, time and place of birth.

“Knowing the accurate time is important here because even 10 minutes can make a difference in the sign,” Verkhotina explains.

“Once you have the data, you can trust astrology software to calculate it for you. There are a lot of natal chart calculators online, so you can just search ‘rising sign calculator,'” Verkhotina says.

Pro tip: Verkhotina suggests reading horoscopes from your rising sign instead of your sun sign, saying it will likely give more personalized insights on which areas of your life might be impacted by current cosmic events.

“A moon sign describes the position of the moon on the zodiac wheel at the moment of your birth,” Verkhotina says.

She explains that the moon in astrology symbolizes:

“The moon sign helps you better understand how these themes demonstrate themselves in your life,” Verkhotina says.

Unlike the rising sign, you don’t have to have the precise time of birth to know your moon sign, although Verkhotina says it’s still recommended.

You can also use an online calculator to find your moon sign or refer to the ephemeris — a table showing the daily positions of planets.

Verkhotina describes the sun sign as the most important planet in your chart.

“It’s the center of your vitality, your ego, consciousness, and individuality at its core. That’s why it’s the most commonly known element in astrology,” she says.

It represents the zodiac sign the sun was in at the time of your birth, which Verkhotina says gives your individuality certain qualities associated with its specific sign.

“It’s important to understand that although the sun is a huge element in astrology, it doesn’t cover the nuances of one’s character,” Verkhotina explains.

Instead, she says it just represents overall traits.

Verkhotina adds that the specifics of your character are covered in the rest of your astrological chart. “This is why sometimes no two leos are the same,” she says.

This one is easy peasy — you don’t have to have your time or place of birth.

“The sun cycle is very similar every year, so you can look it up by the date, month and year of your birth. Each sign corresponds to a calendar date that year,” Verkhotina says.

Here’s each astro sign, in a nutshell, according to Verkhotina.

Your sun sign is important, but your moon and rising signs add extra details.

Your rising sign reflects your identity and how others see you, while your moon sign reveals your emotions and behavior.

To find these signs, you can use online birth chart calculators. Just make sure you have your birth date and time handy for accurate results.

Last medically reviewed on August 2, 2024

#9091. Sabine Marcelis takes a moment to reflect in first museum exhibition

Photography by Umberto Romito and Ivan Šuta

Sabine Marcelis has a knack for creating viral objects, from IKEA’s most-sold light to her mesmerising Candy Cube tables. Now, the designer is revealing the method behind her “magic” in an exhibition at Zürich‘s Museum für Gestaltung.

Light and Color is the first museum show dedicated entirely to Marcelis‘s work since she founded her studio 15 years ago.

In that time, the Rotterdam-based Kiwi has gone from being a student at the Design Academy Eindhoven to one of the most prolific and in-demand designers working today.

“This is the first time a museum has brought so much of my work together in one place,” Marcelis told Dezeen. “I’m always so preoccupied with what’s next that I don’t like to look back so much, but it’s amazing to have this moment to actually stop and look back for a minute.”

The show brings together 17 key pieces from the last decade and a half, going as far back as Tall Stripe – the first of many mirrors – and her signature resin Candy Cubes, which first catapulted the designer to international acclaim in 2014.

But Marcelis is adamant it should not be considered a retrospective.

“I didn’t want the show to feel like a retrospective in the sense of a chronological archive,” she said. “I wanted to select a variety of projects that each show a different way of working with light and colour.”

Rather than chronologically, the exhibits are arranged by colour, blending into each other like the soft gradients she favours in works like her curved glass chaise longues for the Barcelona Pavilion.

Her favourite materials – glass, resin and stone – recur throughout the exhibition, with carefully placed spotlights showing off the play of reflections and shadows the designer has learned to elicit through years of experimentation.

A prime example is her Lokum coffee table for Acerbis, stacked on top of each other on a curved wall to show the gradients of colour and water-like reflections created when the glass is seen at different angles and levels of illumination.

There are also two room-scale installations, reminiscent of Yayoi Kusama‘s Infinity Mirror Rooms, throwing back endless reflections of Marcelis’s viral IKEA “donut lamp” and the towering three-metre-tall Column lava lamp for Mathmos.

For the show’s curator Damian Fopp, these are less about Instagram bait and more about allowing visitors to experience the full visual effect of these objects in real life, rather than through a screen.

“Her work circulated widely as images, but no institution had looked at it as a whole,” he said. “This also made it interesting to shift the conversation back from online to physical.”

“And we wanted to show what lies behind those calm, effortless images: the testing, prototyping and production that I discovered when I visited her studio in Rotterdam.”

A mini-documentary and a book commissioned for the exhibition pull back the curtain on what it takes to create these perception-bending pieces with her team.

Over the years, these have become more ambitious in scale as well as sustainability, pivoting to 99 per cent biobased resin for her production and creating installations for the likes of Coachella and Apple HQ,

But no matter the size of the project, Marcelis says that materials remain her North Star.

“I wrote a one-sentence summary of what my studio does ten years ago,” she remembered. “‘A studio for material, installation and object design. Forever in search of magical moments within materiality and manufacturing processes to create unexpected experiences.'”

“I wouldn’t change that sentence today if I had to make the same summary again.”

Photography by Umberto Romito and Ivan Šuta

Airline pricing is driven by demand, and demand follows predictable weekly patterns. Business travelers fly Monday mornings and Thursday or Friday afternoons. Leisure travelers fly Friday evenings and return Sunday afternoons. The days with the least demand — and therefore the lowest fares — are Tuesday, Wednesday, and Saturday.

Here is what the aggregate pricing data from Google Flights, Hopper, and airline fare databases consistently shows:

The savings are most pronounced on popular leisure routes (New York to Miami, Chicago to Los Angeles, any route to Las Vegas or Orlando) where weekend demand is highest. On less popular routes or business-heavy corridors, the day-of-week effect is smaller. The practical takeaway: if you have any flexibility, fly out on Tuesday or Wednesday and return on a Tuesday or Wednesday. A couple flying round-trip can save $100 to $400 simply by shifting their travel days.

One important note: these are averages across thousands of routes. Individual route pricing varies based on competition, seasonal demand, and airline capacity decisions. Always compare specific dates using Google Flights rather than assuming Tuesday is cheapest for your exact itinerary.

The old advice about booking flights on a specific day of the week — typically Tuesday at 1 AM — is a myth that has never been supported by data. Airlines use dynamic pricing algorithms that adjust fares thousands of times per day based on demand, competition, and remaining seat inventory. There is no magical booking day.

What does matter is how far in advance you book. Here are the optimal booking windows based on aggregate data from Hopper, Google Flights, and CheapAir analyses of millions of fares:

The general pattern is that prices start high when flights first open (9-11 months out), drop to their lowest point in the 1-3 month window as airlines compete for bookings, then spike in the final 2-3 weeks as remaining seats become scarce. Holiday travel follows a compressed version of this pattern with higher floor prices throughout.

The most reliable strategy is not to try timing the absolute bottom but to set fare alerts and buy when the price drops to a level you consider a good deal. Waiting for a slightly lower fare risks watching prices climb permanently as departure approaches.

The right tools eliminate the need to manually check prices. Here is what works best and how to use each one:

Fare alerts are the single most effective strategy for the time-constrained FI-minded traveler. Set alerts on Google Flights for every trip you are considering in the next 6 months. You will receive email notifications when prices drop, and you can book immediately without daily searching. This passive approach consistently saves $50 to $300 per ticket.

For those building a travel rewards strategy, credit card travel portals (Chase Ultimate Rewards, Amex Travel, Capital One Travel) sometimes offer slightly better prices than booking direct. More importantly, points earned through everyday spending can cover flights entirely. A card earning 2x points on all purchases turns $25,000 in annual spending into 50,000 points — enough for 1-2 round-trip domestic flights. The FI approach to travel rewards is not to spend more to earn points, but to redirect spending you would do anyway through a rewards-earning card and let the points accumulate passively.

The single biggest predictor of cheap airfare is not when you book or which tool you use — it is how flexible you are with dates and destinations. Google Flights date grid and Skyscanner everywhere search exist specifically to help flexible travelers find the cheapest options. Being willing to fly on a Tuesday instead of a Friday, or to visit Portugal instead of France, routinely saves 30-50% compared to fixed-date, fixed-destination searches. For FI-minded travelers, flexibility is a skill that pays dividends on every trip.

Tuesday and Wednesday are consistently the cheapest days to fly domestically, with fares typically 15-25% below Friday and Sunday prices. Saturday can also be a good value for departures. The savings are largest on popular leisure routes where weekend demand creates the biggest price swings.

No. The idea that booking on Tuesday at midnight gets you the best price is a myth. Airlines adjust prices thousands of times per day using dynamic pricing algorithms. What matters is booking within the optimal window (1-3 months out for domestic flights) and setting fare alerts to catch price drops.

For domestic flights, 1 to 3 months before departure is the sweet spot. For international flights, 2 to 8 months is optimal. Holiday travel should be booked 2 to 4 months ahead. Booking too early (6+ months for domestic) or too late (under 2 weeks) typically results in higher prices.

Sometimes. Spirit, Frontier, and other ultra-low-cost carriers advertise base fares 40-60% below major airlines but charge separately for carry-on bags ($35-$65), seat selection ($5-$50), and other extras. For a traveler with no checked bag and no seat preference, budget carriers save real money. For families or anyone checking bags, compare total cost including all fees — major airlines are often competitive.

Yes. The cheapest times to fly domestically are January (after the 7th), February (excluding Valentine week), early March, late April, September, October, and early November. The most expensive periods are the weeks around Thanksgiving, Christmas, spring break, and the peak summer window from mid-June through mid-August.

Travel rewards cards earn points on everyday spending that can be redeemed for flights. A card earning 2x points on all purchases turns $25,000 in annual spending into enough points for 1-2 domestic round trips. The FI-aligned approach is to use a rewards card for purchases you would make anyway (groceries, gas, utilities) and let points accumulate passively — never spend more just to earn points.

Finding cheap flights comes down to three principles: be flexible with dates (fly Tuesday or Wednesday for 15-25% savings), book in the right window (1-3 months for domestic, 2-8 for international), and let technology do the searching (Google Flights fare alerts catch drops automatically). Combined with a travel rewards card that earns points on everyday spending, these strategies make air travel significantly more affordable without requiring hours of research. Set your alerts, stay flexible, and book when the price is right.

#9089. gustaf westman gives disney’s mickey & friends his signature chunky, colorful forms

the swedish designer translates familiar cartoon silhouettes into rounded household objects from colorful tableware to collectible furniture.

Swedish designer Gustaf Westman has teamed up with Disney to turn Mickey Mouse and his friends into a collection of sculptural furniture and household objects. Mickey’s oversized ears become a mirror, Donald Duck takes the shape of a colorful bookstand, and Goofy’s silhouette finds its way into furniture. Westman borrows details from the animated characters and reworks them through the rounded forms and exaggerated proportions that have come to define his Stockholm-based studio.

Gustaf Westman’s furniture has always had a cartoonish quality, with chunky silhouettes and bright colors that give ordinary household objects a more playful vibe. The designer works here with characters whose visual identities are already built around simple, recognizable shapes. The collection spans smaller pieces of tableware and decorative accessories, and extends all the way to sofas and larger furniture.

Among the smaller of Gustaf Westman’s objects for Disney is Mickey’s Trouser Vase, a bright red vessel shaped like the character’s shorts, complete with oversized white buttons. The Mickey Pipe Mirror takes an equally direct approach, tracing the outline of his round ears in polished metal tubing. Meanwhile, Donald Duck is interpreted as a sculptural bookstand, with his sailor hat, red bow tie and yellow feet arranged into a colorful composition of geometric forms.

Throughout the collection, recognizable character details take on entirely new functions. Donald’s sailor hat becomes a cup, while Goofy’s distinctive silhouette informs a sculptural vase. Mickey and Minnie also appear across a range of tableware, with their ears and accessories translated into the designer‘s usual bulbous forms.

The collaboration expands into larger furniture with the Mickey and Minnie sofas, whose exaggerated curves bring the characters into the living room. Westman also introduces a Goofy Coffee Table and Donald Shelf, building familiar animated silhouettes into functional objects. A Mickey Bar Cart continues the collection’s exploration of cartoon-inspired furniture, with forms that feel equally at home in Westman’s existing catalog.

Across the range, Westman uses surprisingly few details to suggest each character. A pair of rounded ears or a particular combination of colors is often enough. This approach allows the objects to retain their own sculptural identities, while drawing on the familiarity of Disney’s animated world. The characters become part of the furniture’s geometry, shaping the way each piece occupies space.

#9088. Yinka Ilori reveals Tottenham Hotspur away shirt

Photography courtesy of Tottenham Hotspur Football Club

British-Nigerian designer Yinka Ilori has collaborated with Premier League football team Tottenham Hotspur to create a customised version of the club’s colourful away shirt.

Ilori reimagined the colourful away shirt, which was designed by Nike with a pattern of “never-before-seen visuals inspired by never-before-seen destinations”, by adding a graphic to the front and back.

On the front, in the position the sponsor logo is usually located, Ilori designed a circular motif combining the football club’s initials – THFC – with an abbreviation for London and the postcode for Tottenham, LDN17.

The lettering is bright orange with a white background.

On the rear of the shirt, Ilori created a graphic in his typical playful style around the letters COYS, which stands for Come On You Spurs.

Encircling the letters are the words “I know I am, I’m sure I am”, with the words “We are Tottenham wherever we go” around the whole graphic.

All of the lettering uses Ilori’s custom typeface, which was designed by type foundry British Standard Type for the designer in 2024.

According to the designer, who grew up in north London where the Populous-designed Tottenham Hotspur stadium is located, the collaboration aims to demonstrate the power of football to unite people.

“This project is a celebration of belonging and the power of football to bring people together,” said Ilori.

“For me, football is about the wider culture and the incredible sense of unity that comes from standing on the terraces, chanting alongside thousands of others,” he continued.

“I wanted the design to honour Tottenham Hotspur’s heritage while capturing that collective joy and spirit. The ‘Never Far From Home’ message really resonated with me, reflecting how football has the power to make you feel at home, wherever you are.”

The shirt is the latest design from the designer who has recently collaborated with brands including Brabantia and Veuve Clicquot.

Ilori also recently created a homeware and furniture collection for department store Dunelm.

#9087. Yoga and Overweight: Health Benefits and Tips for Getting Started

Part of the beauty of yoga is its accessibility for everyone. Yoga practitioners come in all shapes and sizes and are hella modifiable. If you have overweight, there’s 100% a place for you in the world of downward dogs, crescent lunges, and resting pigeons.

Check out these benefits of yoga for overweight.

For wellness, you’d be hard-pressed to find a more holistic practice than yoga. Your physical and mental health can get a boost from busting out your mat.

The limb-stretching, muscle-engaging, bodyweight-bearing nature of yoga has many physical benefits.

For starters, yoga may enhance your metabolism. An older study found that people who practiced had greater metabolic efficiency and lower weight than non-yogis.

It’s clear, too, that yoga’s combo of cardio and strength torches calories. A 160-pound person can burn around 180 calories per hour, popping in and out of poses. A 2021 study revealed that both Hatha and vinyasa yoga led to weight loss, with an average of 3.4 kilograms (7.5 pounds) lost over a 6-month.

Extra strength and flexibility are two other well-known upsides of the practice. Research shows that even sedentary folks can build these elements of fitness by taking up yoga. One study showed that, after 8 weeks of practicing at least twice a week (180 minutes), people with no prior yoga experience had greater muscle strength, endurance, flexibility, and cardio-respiratory fitness.

On the surface, yoga might look like mere stretching — but the practice goes far beyond the physical. Yoga engages the mind in all sorts of ways that may have benefits for overweight.

By training your brain toward calm and focus, yoga sessions encourage mindfulness. A mindful outlook can have far-reaching effects in multiple areas of life, like promoting mindful eating and greater body awareness.

As a form of self-care, yoga can also promote a healthier body image. In a 2018 study, young adults who made it a habit reported higher satisfaction levels with their bodies. Better self-esteem and motivation have also been linked to the practice.

Then, too, yoga’s stress-relieving effects might follow you off the mat and into the dining room. Some research has found that people who do yoga binge eat less often.

Wanna get started with yoga but aren’t sure how? We got you.

It all starts with setting realistic goals and expectations. If you’ve never practiced before, you won’t be pretzel-ing yourself into challenging poses like scorpion or crow overnight — and that’s OK. Consider setting smaller, step-wise goals, such as attending a 30-minute class twice a week or mastering a few basic poses. Little by little, you’ll work your way up to a more advanced practice.

It’s also wise to select a class (or video) for beginners. Check your gym or yoga studio’s schedule for introductory sessions, and don’t be afraid to let an instructor know before class that you may need some modifications. Most are happy to provide adaptations to make the class a better experience for beginners.

Meanwhile, if you’re pursuing a yoga practice for weight loss, remember to pair it with other healthy lifestyle practices for best results. Though stretching and holding poses burn calories, yoga might not take you to your weight loss goal alone. A balanced diet, cardio exercise, and sufficient sleep are other keys to achieving a healthy weight.

Yoga stereotypes of scantily clad gym babes in impossible contortions might make you feel somewhat intimidated about in-person classes. If you’re concerned that a gym session will make you self-conscious, start with an at-home practice. (YouTube is a treasure trove of classes and instructors explicitly geared for people with overweight.) All by yourself in your living room, there’s no one to impress.

Or, if you’re up for in-person yoga, let your instructor know your needs again. Modifications are always possible.

No matter where you practice, credit yourself for showing up for your health. And, at the beginning of your session, don’t forget to set an intention you find motivating or encouraging, such as “I am caring for my body” or “I am worthy of love and respect.”

Overweight doesn’t have to be a barrier to taking up yoga. Start small, knowing that you’ll get more comfortable with each session. With all the physical and mental health benefits a yoga practice provides — and all the modifications that make it more accessible — it’s worth a try, regardless of weight.

Last medically reviewed on August 31, 2024

#9086. Former workshop converted into contemporary Japanese home with "a sense of the passage of time"

Japanese studio Akio Isshiki Architects has transformed the home and workshop of a sheet-metal craftsperson in the castle town of Tatsuno into a modern house with a latticed wooden gate.

Architect Akio Isshiki, the founder of the eponymous studio, said he had to take a lot of different aspects into consideration when designing the project.

Among them was the location, as the two-storey home is located in a historic town known for being built around a medieval mountain castle.

“The project explores an architecture that responds naturally to the many contexts and conditions surrounding the house: the historic streetscape of the former castle town, traces of the former owner’s work as a sheet-metal craftsman, the client’s wishes, and practical constraints such as building regulations and structural requirements,” Isshiki told Dezeen.

For example, while the client had initially wanted a deck that would be connected to the dining room, the compact site made such a design difficult.

Instead, Isshiki removed part of the existing interior of the dining room to create a terrace space, which also includes a traditional-style engawa platform to connect the home with the garden.

Here, the studio added a sliding glass door that was designed so that its frame is hidden in the wall when it is closed, creating the impression of a fully open space.

Isshiki also wanted the 144-square-metre contemporary home to nod to more traditional Japanese houses.

“To sit comfortably within the townscape that retains the character of a former castle town, the spatial principles of traditional machiya – Japanese old townhouses – have been incorporated into this contemporary residence,” he explained.

“Examples include a long approach leading towards a bright garden at the back of the house, and an engawa, a narrow platform that connects the interior with the garden.”

The former workshop in front of the house was treated as a public-facing space. Where it looks onto the street, Isshiki added a large latticed, sliding gate, made from cedar, as well as a narrow entrance porch.

Inside, this multi-functional space becomes almost like an enclosed terrace. Here, Isshiki also added a small wooden toilet, inspired by those found in traditional machiya houses.

The studio kept a number of objects that were found in the old workshop, including a metal ring that now decorates a handrail next to the indoor staircase.

Isshiki relocated this staircase so that it sits at the front of the house, in the old workshop space – one of the biggest changes made to the layout of the house. A stone underneath the first step provides a space to remove footwear.

Isshiki’s studio used wood throughout the renovation, as the original building was made from timber and this material worked best with the existing neighbourhood, including a historic shrine that stands directly across from the house.

“The newly added wood, including the doors, is cedar, which is also the primary wood used in the original structure,” Isshiki said.

“Cedar is one of the most widely used types of wood in Japan and is readily available,” he continued.

“The contrast between the lighter new cedar and the existing cedar, which has darkened with age, brings a sense of the passage of time to the house.”

Akio Isshiki Architects also used earthen plasterwork in the home to create a tactile feel, while Tunisian tiles add decorative patterns in the kitchen. Here, the studio also created a built-in, combined wooden dining table and work surface.

On the top floor, which has a bedroom, living room and guest room, the studio mostly kept the original layout.

However, it added a sunken study space and a tokonoma, a recessed area used to display flowers and pieces of art.

“Through careful consideration of spatial dimensions, light, connections to the outdoors, materials, details, and relationships between spaces, the aim was to create a home that feels comfortable as a whole,” Isshiki concluded about the renovation.

His studio has previously designed a charred-cedar-clad house in Osaka and married old and new within a combined home and restaurant.
