#9042. It’s Nia Long’s Moment—Again

There is a specific kind of vertigo that comes with leaving a movie theater in the middle of the day. The world is suddenly too bright, too loud, and slightly unreal. You have, after all, been inside someone else’s carefully constructed reality for two hours. And then you’re back outside, blinking into the afternoon light, not quite returned to yourself, the movie still clinging to you like perfume. It’s in this particular state that I meet Nia Long for an early lunch in a quiet corner at the Chateau Marmont.

I have just seen Michael (the new Michael Jackson biopic) a month ahead of its April release. I’m still thinking about the film when Long, who plays Jackson family matriarch Katherine Jackson, arrives looking chic but low-key in an oversized blazer, wide-leg jeans, and a Miu Miu baseball cap pulled low. As we ease ourselves into the conversation, I’m struck by the strange doubling effect of the movie vertigo: the woman before me and the woman I have just watched, layered like two transparencies held up to the light.

On screen, Long plays Katherine Jackson with a studied stillness. The first time we see her, watching her boys rehearse, the frame holds on her loving face for just a few beats. She says almost nothing. She doesn’t have to. Juxtaposed to Colman Domingo’s blustering portrayal of Joe Jackson and Jaafar Jackson’s uncanny performance as his late uncle Michael, Long has found a way to make silence load-bearing. Restraint is the most visible thing in any scene she occupies.

In person she seems the opposite of restrained. She is blunt but also quite warm, with a dry sense of humor and a deep well of emotional intelligence. She is very much a Scorpio. She notices everything. And, in playing Mrs. Jackson (who is still with us at the age of 95), Long has tapped into the part of herself that knows how to let silence do the work. The word she reaches for when she talks about the experience of playing the matriarch—a word she will return to several times during our conversation—is grace.

“There have been moments in my life where I’ve been required to be more graceful than I’ve ever had to be in the past,” she says. “And that requires a sense of really being able to dig deep into some sort of self-examination. Like, what do I stand for? What’s important to me, ultimately, regardless of Hollywood, the noise? And number one, for me personally, my children come before anything. And so I think when you look at Michael’s journey, and you look at Katherine’s journey, the only way you thrive and survive is through a tremendous amount of grace.” She pauses. “What I think I learned from her is that sometimes grace is really quiet.”

Long occupies a place in our cultural memory that few actors do. She is, for a certain generation, the platonic ideal of ’90s Fine, a phrase that’s not only about beauty or aesthetic but also about a certain feeling. Watching her as Nina in Love Jones or Jordan in The Best Man or Lisa in The Fresh Prince of Bel-Air, you conjure up a place and time and attitude that feels synonymous with Long. Of course, there is the image, and then there is the human sitting across from me, eating her go-to order of salmon with a side of mustard. And as she does, I ask what she thinks about the iconography and the nostalgia that surrounds her.

“My commitment to work is not for accolades or attention, or even to be famous, quite honestly,” she says. “But I do think because of my commitment to truth and purpose, there is a thing, and I don’t know what that thing is, that people see in my work. And it makes them feel good. It makes them feel inspired. It makes them feel like they know me.”

In a fickle Hollywood landscape that’s even more fickle when it comes to Black actors, Long doesn’t take the longevity and love she’s cultivated for granted. “There's highs and lows,” Long admits. “I’m having a great year, but I don’t know what’s happening next year.”

Long has starred in several iconic Black films, and she’s always been intentional about how she plays her characters. Much like with the Katherine Jackson role, she creates a version of the person that feels, to her, like something true.

“The only strategy I have in this game is my bank account. Let’s strategize how we’re going to make money and create generational wealth. That is where I’m strategic.” She laughs, scratches her palm. “My hand just started itching the minute I said money. That’s a good thing. Maybe something’s happening. Something’s coming.”

Once she’s in it, though, the work becomes something more personal. “I work hard to make sure that when I represent us, it’s not just someone putting their agenda on me. Whether it’s my hair, my makeup, my wardrobe, my lines.”

Now that her eldest son is in his 20s and her youngest son, 14, is old enough to stay home by himself, the actor feels ready to expand in all directions. She wants to continue to produce more films, craft new stories both behind and in front of the camera. She tells me about a new film she’s just wrapped shooting in New York, Don’t Ever Wonder, a romantic dramedy (“If that even exists anymore”) three years in the making. It will feature her onscreen reunion with Love Jones leading man Larenz Tate. Directed by Eugene Ashe and featuring an ensemble that includes Blair Underwood, Susan Kelechi Watson, and Algee Smith, the film is all about second acts.

“This is not a continuation of Love Jones,” she emphasizes. “This is a continuation of love, and of what happens once you’ve had your kids, they’re off to college, and you’re empty nesters. And that’s kind of where the story begins. There’s a lot of funny and there’s a lot of heartbreak, and I think it’s a really honest story.”

In talking to Long, I get the sense that honesty and truth is what she values most in the stories she tells. It’s what she values in life as well. Perhaps that’s what compels me, somewhere in the middle of our lunch, to unmask. I mention that I am conducting the interview a little out of sorts, having just ended a 12-year relationship.

“Okay, but when was it really over?” she asks.

"You didn’t have to gag me like that!" I say.

She laughs. I tell her that I am trying to imagine what life will look like—what I will look like—on the other side of this break-up. That’s when the idea of grace comes up again.

In 2022, Long went through that peculiar part of fame where something private becomes public overnight: her partner’s cheating scandal that resulted in the end of their 13-year relationship. She doesn’t have to go too deep into it if she doesn’t want to, I assure her, but the actor doesn’t shy away. On the other side of the experience with her ex, with whom she now has a healthy coparenting relationship, she has an unflinching clarity about the whole ordeal.

“The amount of pouring into myself that I’ve done is strong and mighty and intentional. I’ve now identified the things that I need to work on and the things that I need to heal. But I have also identified what is intolerable.”

That clarity has been hard-won. When the cheating scandal happened, there was a groundswell of support from fans, a protectiveness over Long as a woman and as a cultural touchstone. But in the instances that she’s talked publicly about it, including in our conversation, I’m struck by how her gratitude for the support is always tempered with nuance.

“I’m proud of myself for giving so much grace. For being able to say people make mistakes and things happen. It’s life. When the stakes are high, the news is big. I can’t do anything about that, but I don’t have to protect my ego in any of this.” She says all this very matter-of-factly, which is the only way she seems capable of saying things.

In the same straightforward tone she suggests I write out everything I need to say to my ex without sending it, because ultimately “it’s not about another person’s behavior. It’s about your bottom line and the magnitude in which you’re committed to self-love,” she says. “I don’t think it's healthy to hold onto things because then you’re just walking around with this burdensome energy. It could be writing it down. It could be meditation. It could be prayer. There’s a lot of ways to manage the noise. But you don’t have to respond to the noise with the undercurrent of your own trauma.”

I write down this last sentence because it is useful, but also because it is the key to something I’ve been watching Long do across the whole of our conversation: find the lesson in whatever she is given.

Long is working on her first memoir, a process she describes as one of the “biggest, bravest, challenging” things she’s ever done. It’s been a two-year process, a constant negotiation with her own relationship to letting go.

“I can read something I wrote two years ago and go: ‘Oh no, that’s not actually how I feel about that now.’” Long’s father, Doughtry Long Jr., a poet who died in 2020, told her the hardest thing about writing is knowing when to stop. “And I’m like: When is that going to happen? Because I haven’t gotten there yet.”

The memoir takes her back to Iowa City, where she spent six years of her childhood while her mother attended university. She was born in Brooklyn, in a Trinidadian household where everyone on the block was Black. Living in the Midwest during her formative years, she encountered few other Black girls, which disoriented her relationship to race.

“In writing this memoir, I realized the impact that experience had on my own view of beauty,” she says. “And my own self-acceptance of being a pretty brown-skinned little girl growing up in Iowa. I thought I was beautiful because my mother said it and my family said it, but the world told me something different.” She lets that sit. “So to now be a face for Estée Lauder, it’s kind of ironic, because I didn’t feel beautiful until Black Hollywood said I was beautiful.”

That an entire generation of Black women found a reflection of Black beauty in Nia Long while Long herself was still waiting to see it tells us something about how beauty standards work, and how much labor goes into transforming them. Nineties Fine, after all, did not emerge from a vacuum. It was a corrective, Black Hollywood’s answer to a century of the larger industry rendering Black women invisible or, worse, making us visible in ways that were wholly out of our control. Long’s most iconic characters—and indeed, Long herself—reflected a new idea of beauty, of the Black leading lady, expansive in some ways and still restrictive in others. Now, some 30 years on, Long embodies a new facet of being a Black woman in Hollywood.

“Black don’t crack” gets lobbed at Black women constantly, ostensibly as a compliment, but one that sometimes erases the very real pressure that comes with aging—especially aging on a public stage, especially when people have a particular image of you stored in amber.

But Long is not interested in pretending that the body is not a thing that transforms. “I’m 55. I got hormonal stuff going. Your body shifts, changes. It’s a whole new body.” She is not wistful about this. She also ate the truffle parmesan fries and does not appear remotely conflicted about it. She mentions the coming press tour for Michael, how she wants to be in beautiful gowns but she also wants French fries.

“I don’t deprive myself of anything that I want,” she says. “I find the balance.”

Beauty was never her primary currency, she says. It had to be something else, other inheritances: her father’s curiosity, her mother’s fierce self-possession. Tattooed and free-spirited, her mother wore leg warmers in the middle of summer because they matched her outfit, and she did not care for one second what anyone thought about that. Embarrassed, Long would beg her mother to take them off. She never did. As an adult, Long sees the power and freedom in that.

Our plates are carted away. Long has to leave soon for a pizza party at home with her youngest son and his friends. Before she goes, I ask her what freedom, at this point, is to her.

“Being able to do what you want to do when you want to do it, because it serves your spirit, not what everyone else thinks you need to be or should be,” she says. That type of freedom, Long adds, doesn’t require an audience.“You don’t have to have anyone else’s permission to do what you love. And it doesn’t have to be on the big stage. It could be in your kitchen. I know I have freedom right now to make a pizza. I’m going to do it.”

#9041. Six standout projects unveiled at Designart Tokyo 2026

As the 10th anniversary edition of Designart Tokyo gets underway, Jane Englefield reports on six highlights from the citywide festival of Japanese creativity.

Designart Tokyo opened on 30 October and will remain open across Tokyo until 8 November.

Around 150 projects by exhibitors from 13 countries are on display at various galleries and other pop-up locations throughout the city.

This year’s main exhibition venue is the former site of the Tokyo Expressway, also known as the KK Line, a portion of which is now an elevated park in the heart of Ginza.

Designart Tokyo’s first dedicated design store is also located on site, selling works from brands including Nendo and Alessi, as well as designers Ronan Bouroullec and Kwangho Lee.

Read on for six of our highlights from the event:

Pulling Apart is a novel adhesive on display as part of the Daikanyama exhibition Separation: Designed to Come Apart, which includes various products created to allow for fluid disassembly and recycling.

Tokyo studio Nomura created the project with the knowledge that, when glue-based adhesives are applied to timber or metal, they are often difficult or impossible to remove. This can mean that materials suffer indelible marks or cannot be recycled at the end of their life.

Nomura’s adhesive is a strong but flexible tape, which firmly holds heavy materials in place. But once the tape is tugged, it stretches and comes away easily.

“Leave one end within reach behind the plinth or under the tabletop, and when the time comes, a single pull undoes the whole thing,” said Nomura.

The tape was developed with easy-disassembly bonding technology developed by Aica Kogyo Company and is still in the prototype phase.

“Peco poco” is a common Japanese onomatopoeia describing a growling stomach.

Experimental design studio Howdunit used the phrase as its starting point for this table lamp, which can be manually unfolded like an accordion thanks to a small hook built into the top of the shade.

Made from delicate layers of gauzy textile, the light opens with a “rhythmic ‘peco poco’ motion” and can be set at various heights.

“By continually asking how things are made, we aim to discover new possibilities in design,” said Howdunit founders Haruto Kamijo and Sho Tasaki.

Forest: Perspectives by Oji Holdings and We+

Tokyo paper manufacturer Oji Holdings is presenting an exhibition in Ginza that meditates on our perspectives on forests.

The manufacturer asked nine professionals, from designers and wood specialists to a writer and a chef, to visit the network of forests it manages and share their individual responses to the landscape.

Among them are delicately whittled spoons made from fallen branches and wood sheets crafted out of bark using a process similar to making washi paper.

The exhibition was laid out in an encyclopedic display designed by local studio We+, founded by Toshiya Hayashi and Hokuto Ando.

Founded in 2021, Tokyo-based 21B Studio is presenting an exhibition at Shibuya’s brutalist-style Tiers Gallery.

Box is the first solo show by the young studio, conceived to demonstrate the myriad ways we can create the humble paper box through various folds and incisions.

The studio is giving out an intricately designed flatpack poster advertising the exhibition, which, once assembled, resembles the geometric architecture of Tiers Gallery itself.

Over in Tokyo Midtown, design master’s student Cecil Nabenashi is presenting a playful exhibition of vases and bowls made of deep-fried paper and fibres.

Nabenashi looked to tempura, Japanese food that is coated in batter and deep-fried in oil, when creating the project.

His goal was to experiment with his “tempura” technique to see if it could provide a long-lasting finish for design objects, using a “batter” he developed from a specially developed blend of non-edible ingredients.

The designer told Dezeen that he plans for his next challenge to be a deep-fried garment.

Industrial Romanticism is an exhibition on display at Minato’s Axis Gallery, Japan’s first dedicated design gallery founded in 1981.

The show is a group exhibition held by designers Yoshiki Matsuyama and Ryota Yokozeki, who asked eight leading Japanese companies to take part.

In-house designers at each of the companies, including bathroom brand Toto and camera maker Fujifilm, created prototypes of recognisable products with an imaginative twist.

Among the designs is a piano made by Ryusuke Baba of musical instrument maker Yamaha. Baba created the piano from pieces of timber that would normally be rejected for an instrument, creating a keyboard with an offbeat sound.

Designart Tokyo 2026 takes place from 30 October to 8 November 2026 at various locations across Tokyo, Japan. See Dezeen Events Guide for an up-to-date list of architecture and design events taking place around the world.

#9040. Khao Phra Tamnak House / SPACE | STORY | STUDIO

Text description provided by the architects. Set on the gentle hillside of Khao Phra Tamnak, the house is conceived through a flexible design diagram rather than a predetermined architectural form. The project begins with the conditions of the place and the lives to be accommodated: a gradual change in land level, the family's need for generous and usable flat spaces, the principles of Feng Shui, and the presence of neighboring homes. These factors are not treated as separate constraints. They are brought together in a framework that can be tested, adjusted, and extended.

#9038. How to ‘Quiet Quit’ Your Mom

You’re probably familiar with the term quiet quitting. For a while, that little phrase has been used to describe the experience of executing the bare minimum at work without actually leaving your job: You do just enough to get by but never rise above that benchmark to prove yourself or exceed expectations. It’s a strategy that can keep you employed while preserving your mental and emotional energy.

The term has since been applied to other parts of life, like relationships. And, yes, it could also apply to the one you have with your mom. Though you’re probably not collecting paychecks here, maintaining a relationship with your mother may connect you to important resources you need to get by. Maybe your mom really does play a big role in your finances, or she’s your source of health insurance. She could also be a connection to your culture or other family members that you don’t want to distance yourself from. Logistics aside, you might just want some distance from your mom without sacrificing your emotional connection. As I learned from reporting my book Motherf*cked: How to Keep Your Mother’s Toxic Drama From Ruining Your Life, those are all solid reasons to maintain a relationship that leaves you exhausted.

Going low-contact is pretty much what it sounds like: staying in touch with minimal contact. However, there’s no official definition, therapist Whitney Goodman, LMFT, told me in an interview for Motherf*cked. For some, it could look like avoiding one-on-one visits but checking in via text, email, quarterly phone calls, or greeting cards. Or you could catch up in person while avoiding the details of your life. The frequency of low-contact contact varies too. Some would say talking once a week is low-contact for them. Others might say once a year.

The reasons why people go low-contact differ as much as the ways it can look. Generally speaking, taking space can be useful anytime a relationship feels painful or draining. It gives you more time, energy, and emotional bandwidth to take care of yourself and tend to other important parts of your life.

That can be especially helpful in our relationships with our moms, a dynamic that, for many reasons, is often packed with emotional triggers. If spending time with your mom feels exhausting, you’re sick of always stressing about this relationship, or you’ve tried and failed to set boundaries with her in the past, pulling back might be helpful here, Goodman says. If you can relate, here’s how to do that.

Ideally, this process is a series of experiments where you pull back from the relationship in different ways to see what feels good and what doesn’t, Goodman explains. You can then use that information to determine how much contact is too much—or not enough. Here’s how to get started.

Going low-contact is really just setting a boundary, or defining what behavior you will or won’t tolerate. You’re showing others how you want to be treated. Sometimes, people don’t like being restricted and get messy when limits are put on their relationships. Moms can be like that too.

If you’ve already tried to set boundaries with your mom by, say, not answering every one of her calls or telling her that you don’t want to talk about your dating life, now is a good time to reflect on how that went.

Moms who are receptive to those guardrails may be easygoing about any additional boundaries. That could mean you don’t need to cut as many points of contact to feel better about the relationship. On the other hand, if your mom has blown through your boundaries in the past, you might need stronger limitations to protect your peace today. Keep that in mind for the next step.

Again, there is no official criterion defining a low-contact relationship, so don’t get hung up on labels. First, think about how much contact you have now. How often do you spend time together? What does that time look like? What would you change to make this relationship less taxing?

Maybe you see your mom every Sunday, let her come over unannounced, and answer all of her texts—even the ones you’d rather not. Consider which of these interactions take the most out of you, and ask yourself, Would eliminating this point of contact make the relationship less exhausting overall?

You could start small by taking a beat to check in with yourself before responding to your mom’s texts. If you don’t feel like dealing with her at that moment, don’t. If that’s not enough to preserve your energy, maybe you can limit the number of texts you’ll respond to each day or week. You can always change it up later by removing another point of contact, like those unannounced visits, if you need more space (see step five).

You don’t have to formally announce that you’re going low-contact, but giving your mom a heads-up might be useful.

If you’re not worried about your safety and your quiet quitting tactics mean your mom has to change her behavior, then laying out your plans could make sense. Plus, explaining why you put them in place might help you resolve whatever is behind your decision to quiet quit this relationship.

That said, if your version of low-contact doesn’t require anything from your mom, you don’t need to tell her it’s happening, says Goodman. For example, you can hold back information about your life or avoid certain events without discussing it first.

Feel weird about this? I get that, but here’s something to think about: You’ve probably told your mom about the ways she’s hurt you many, many times before, says Goodman. Even if you haven’t explicitly pointed to every single occasion she hurt your feelings, your body language and tone of voice likely have conveyed how her actions impacted you. You may be tired of retelling those painful events, which is why you’d like to avoid another confrontation with your mom. So consider this your permission not to.

Still, your mom might notice you pulling back and ask what’s going on. If she does, you can tell her why you’re not getting into your dating life or attending the family reunion. You don’t have to, though. You’re welcome to make excuses or just say, “Yep, you’re right, I’m not doing that anymore.” You don’t owe her an explanation.

Goodman says the best way to tell how going low-contact is working for you is to check in with your emotions as much as possible. You can write them down in your journal, use a mood- or emotions-tracking app, or bring them up to your therapist.

Yes, the feelings you’re tracking can be related to your mom and quiet quitting her, but don’t forget about all the others, says Goodman. It might not be obvious which feelings are related to your maternal figure and which aren’t. After breaking patterns that existed for a long time, you might get a sense that something is off. Maybe you feel purposeless or lost. Maybe it’s like you forgot something on your way to the airport, but you don’t know what it is.

All of that is normal, says Goodman. So is feeling like you really miss your mom, even if you know you did the right thing. Of course, everyone’s situation is different. Maybe you don’t truly miss her, but miss the idea of a person she’ll never be. When quiet quitting is working, those feelings should come up less frequently and/or become less intense. At the same time, you’ll likely feel some relief. You could notice more peace in your life and more space to focus on things other than your mom.

You can always tweak how much contact you have with your mom. Ideally, this involves a continuous assessment of what’s working and what’s not. If the low-contact plan you’ve established feels sustainable and makes you less obsessive or overwhelmed by the relationship—and your mom is able to abide by your rules—you might have found a solution. Success!

If this version of quiet quitting doesn’t keep your mom from violating your boundaries, emotionally manipulating you, or still leaves you drained, anxious, or depressed, you could level up, says Goodman. That means starting back at step one and quitting other parts of your relationship until you reach a point that feels sustainable.

Remember, the goal is for you to feel less stressed about your interactions with your mom. By finding a routine that works for you, you can protect the parts of your relationship that you love and lose the rest.

#9037. A Garden City in the Caribbean: Planning Belize’s New Capital, Belmopan

Located on the Caribbean coast of Central America, Belize is a small country with an intriguing history. It is bordered by Mexico to the north and Guatemala to the west and south, with the Caribbean Sea along its eastern edge. Known as British Honduras for most of its past, it was formally made into a British colony in 1862, long after its Central American neighbors had won their independence from Spain. As the territory transitioned toward independence, it adopted two symbols of its emerging identity: a new name, Belize, and a new capital, which was built not just to govern the new nation, but also as a way to prevent hurricanes from putting the country's institutional stability at risk.

Located on the Caribbean coast of Central America, Belize is a small country with an intriguing history. It is bordered by Mexico to the north and Guatemala to the west and south, with the Caribbean Sea along its eastern edge. Known as British Honduras for most of its past, it was formally made into a British colony in 1862, long after its Central American neighbors had won their independence from Spain. As the territory transitioned toward independence, it adopted two symbols of its emerging identity: a new name, Belize, and a new capital, which was built not just to govern the new nation, but also as a way to prevent hurricanes from putting the country's institutional stability at risk.

The push for that capital began with a single night of devastation. On October 31, 1961, Hurricane Hattie struck Belize City, the old capital and Caribbean port, destroying roughly 80 percent of its infrastructure and killing nearly 300 people. The extent of the destruction exposed the physical vulnerabilities of maintaining a primary administrative center in a water-surrounded peninsula located at sea level, prompting authorities to re-evaluate the nation's urban future. If British Honduras wanted to enter independence with a capital that could withstand the next storm, it would need to start over somewhere safer. In 1964, the cabinet formally selected an inland site near Roaring Creek Village, located 50 miles west of Belize City, to construct a new capital safe from tropical storm surges and geographically at the center of the new nation of Belize.

#9036. Lagoons will weave through new Egyptian city masterplanned by SOM

International architecture studio SOM has unveiled plans for a new city in Egypt named Alam Al Roum, which will stretch 7.2 kilometres along the Mediterranean coastline.

Set to be built near Marsa Matrouh, the 20.6-square-kilometre masterplan features swimmable lagoons alongside 22 kilometres of seawater-connected lagoons, which will weave through the built environment to support stormwater management.

“The Mediterranean is home to some of the world’s great cities, shaped over centuries by climate, culture and economic forces,” said SOM principal Thomas Hussey.

“Alam Al Roum presents a rare opportunity to imagine a new city from the ground up, one that responds to the realities of climate change while offering an exceptional quality of life.”

SOM designed the masterplan around Egypt’s north coast landscape and climate, orienting buildings and public spaces to take advantage of coastal breezes and sunlight.

The development will be elevated to accommodate changing coastal conditions, while waterfront areas will be protected with natural interventions such as riparian buffers, stormwater wetlands, stabilised dunes and living shorelines.

Designed for developer Qatari Diar, Alam Al Roum will comprise beachfront and lagoon-side neighbourhoods, town centres, areas for hospitality and resorts, golfing facilities, an education district and a business hub.

A grand boulevard will form an urban spine connecting an international marina on the Mediterranean Sea with a mobility hub further inland.

Aiming to establish the city as a year-round cultural destination, Alam Al Roum’s waterfront downtown will contain a cultural pier, lighthouse, amphitheatre, yacht club, mosque, and markets.

The first phase of the city development is expected to commence in 2030, comprising a four-square-kilometre area with a beachfront stretch, open-sea-connected lagoons and a town-centre marina.

“Alam Al Roum represents our vision for a new generation of Mediterranean destinations – one that goes beyond the traditional seasonal resort to create a vibrant, year-round coastal city,” said Qatari Diar CEO Hamad bin Talal Al-Thani.

“We are bringing together nature, the sea, hospitality and everyday life within a carefully planned environment that reflects the unique character of Egypt’s north coast,” he continued.

“Through our partnership with SOM and our global network of experts, we are creating a destination that is rooted in its landscape and climate, while setting a new benchmark for integrated coastal development in the Mediterranean.”

In recent years, Egypt established a new capital city east of Cairo. The initial design concept for the city was designed by SOM and further developed by the international building consultancy Dar al-Handasah Shair & Partners.

Cathay Pacific or Qantas Business Class via Alaska Mileage Plan — no fuel surcharges

Free calculators, a personalized FI roadmap, and a community of 25K+ on the same journey.

Picture this: you're reclining in a fully flat bed at 38,000 feet somewhere over the Pacific, a glass of Château Léoville Barton in hand, watching the Australian coastline slowly materialize through your window. The cabin is hushed. The seat — Cathay Pacific's renowned Business Class throne on the Airbus A350-1000 — cocoons you in a private pod with a sliding door, direct aisle access, and a mattress pad that makes a five-star hotel bed feel like an afterthought. This is the LAX–HKG–SYD route in Cathay Pacific Business Class. And you booked it for 55,000 Alaska Mileage Plan miles. Now consider what the person three rows up in economy paid in cash for their seat — and what the couple beside you in business paid for theirs. A Cathay Pacific Business Class ticket on this route typically retails between **$5,000 and $12,000**. That's not a typo. Premium cabin pricing on transpacific routes is notoriously aggressive, and Australia amplifies it further because of the sheer distance involved. At 55,000 miles for a one-way business class redemption, you're extracting somewhere between **9.1 and 21.8 cents per point (CPP)** — a range that makes most loyalty program strategists stop and stare. The ChooseFI community benchmarks a "good" redemption at 1.5–2 CPP for most programs. You are obliterating that benchmark. At the high end of this range, 55,000 miles is doing the work of $12,000 in cash. That is what the FI mindset calls asymmetric value. This is also a premium *experience*, not just a premium number. Cathay Pacific consistently ranks among the world's top airlines for business class. The A350-1000 is their flagship long-haul aircraft, featuring a 1-2-1 configuration with every single seat having direct aisle access. There are no middle seats. There are no awkward climbs over sleeping strangers. There is a full dine-on-demand menu, a curated wine list, noise-canceling headphones, and a ground service team that treats you like a valued guest before you even board. For the FI traveler, this redemption represents something rare: a genuine luxury experience — the kind that recalibrates your sense of what travel can feel like — made nearly free through a well-understood system. The math works. The experience delivers. And once you've done it, you'll understand exactly why the ChooseFI community talks about this one.

Alaska Mileage Plan is one of the most valuable frequent flyer programs in the world despite being a relatively small airline. The secret is their partner award chart: Alaska uses fixed pricing for partner airline awards, meaning costs do not fluctuate with demand the way dynamic programs do. This creates structural pricing inefficiencies — especially on premium cabin routes to Asia and Oceania — that savvy travelers can exploit. Alaska has partnerships with Cathay Pacific, Qantas, Japan Airlines, Emirates, Fiji Airways, and others. The primary way to earn Alaska miles is through the Alaska Airlines Visa Signature card (Bank of America), through flying, or via Marriott Bonvoy transfers at a 3:1 ratio.

Here's the insight that transforms this from "interesting" to "actionable": Alaska Airlines Mileage Plan uses a fixed partner award chart, and that chart prices Cathay Pacific Business Class to Australia at 55,000 miles one-way — a number that hasn't kept pace with the explosive cash price inflation of premium cabin fares.

Most major U.S. loyalty programs have migrated to dynamic pricing, where award costs fluctuate with cash fare demand. Alaska hasn't done this for partner awards. Their chart is fixed. That means when Cathay Pacific's cash fares spike to $12,000 during Australian school holidays or peak summer travel, your award cost stays exactly where it was: 55,000 miles. This is the pricing inefficiency at the heart of this redemption, and it's why the ChooseFI community treats Alaska Mileage Plan as one of the most valuable programs in the industry.

Alaska Mileage Plan has only one meaningful transfer partner for most people: Marriott Bonvoy, at a ratio of 3 Bonvoy points to 1 Alaska mile. That's a steep ratio — you'll need 165,000 Bonvoy points to generate 55,000 Alaska miles — and transfer times run 1 to 5 days, so plan accordingly. There is no direct credit card transfer path into Alaska Mileage Plan from Chase, Amex, or Citi, which is why the "Easy to Earn" score for this redemption is a 2 out of 5. The miles must be earned directly: through Alaska's co-branded credit card (the Alaska Airlines Visa from Bank of America), through flying Alaska or its partners, or via Marriott transfer.

This is crucial and often overlooked. Alaska charges no fuel surcharges on any partner award bookings. This matters enormously for a Cathay Pacific redemption. If you were to book the same Cathay flight through Cathay's own Asia Miles program or through British Airways Avios, you could face fuel surcharges of $400–$900 or more on top of the points cost. With Alaska, your out-of-pocket cost is taxes and fees only — typically in the range of $50–$150 depending on the routing. That's it. A $12,000 experience for 55,000 miles and roughly $100 in fees.

Alaska allows a free stopover on one-way awards — a benefit that is genuinely rare among U.S. programs. On the LAX–HKG–SYD routing, this means you can build a stopover in Hong Kong at no additional points cost. Spend a few days exploring one of the world's most dynamic cities — the markets of Mong Kok, the skyline from Victoria Peak, the dim sum temples of Kowloon — then board your continuing flight to Sydney. Two destinations. One redemption. Same 55,000 miles.

The 55,000-mile rate applies to both Cathay Pacific and Qantas for business class to Australia. Cathay routes you through Hong Kong (HKG); Qantas has its own metal and routing options. If Cathay availability is thin, checking Qantas can open up alternatives without changing your points cost.

Do not start at Alaska's website. Alaska's own search tool for partner availability can be unreliable for Cathay Pacific. Instead, go to ba.com (British Airways' booking site) and run a one-way business class search for your desired route — for example, LAX to SYD or LAX to HKG. British Airways and Cathay Pacific are oneworld partners, and BA's search engine surfaces Cathay award availability with remarkable accuracy. Look for "Reward" seats in the business class (Club World or equivalent) cabin. Any dates showing availability on BA.com are almost certainly bookable through Alaska as well. Screenshot or note the specific dates before moving on.

Alaska opens its award booking window 331 days in advance. If you're targeting peak travel dates — Australian summer (December–February), for example — set a calendar reminder to search and transfer 331 days ahead. Your miles also never expire in Mileage Plan, which gives you flexibility to accumulate without pressure.

Confirm you have at least 55,000 Alaska miles available. If you're converting Marriott Bonvoy points, you'll need 165,000 Bonvoy points at the 3:1 ratio. Initiate transfers at least one week before you plan to call, as Marriott-to-Alaska transfers can take 1 to 5 days.

Log into your Marriott Bonvoy account, navigate to "Transfer Points," select Alaska Airlines as the recipient program, and enter your Mileage Plan number. Transfer in increments of 3,000 Bonvoy points (yielding 1,000 Alaska miles). Do not transfer until you've confirmed availability in Step 1 — points transfers are generally non-reversible.

This redemption cannot be booked online — Alaska's web portal does not support all partner award bookings, particularly for Cathay Pacific. Call Alaska Airlines at 1-800-252-7522. Tell the agent:

Have your Mileage Plan number, passport information, and a credit card for the taxes and fees ready. The call typically takes 20–40 minutes. Agents are generally knowledgeable, but if you encounter confusion, politely ask for a senior agent or call back.

If Cathay availability is limited on your preferred dates, ask the agent to check Qantas availability to Australia at the same 55,000-mile rate. Qantas Business (The Business) has its own award inventory and may have open seats when Cathay is fully allocated.

If you're routing through Hong Kong on Cathay, explicitly ask the agent to add a free stopover at HKG. This is a program benefit, not a favor — Alaska's routing rules allow one free stopover on one-way awards. Specify how many nights you want in Hong Kong before the continuing flight to Sydney.

The best way to find Cathay Pacific Business Class award availability is through the British Airways website (ba.com). Search for one-way flights from your U.S. gateway to Sydney or Melbourne, and look for dates showing Cathay Pacific-operated flights with Business Class availability. British Airways shows oneworld partner availability more reliably than most tools.

If Cathay Pacific shows no availability on your preferred dates, search for Qantas Business Class on the same route. Qantas availability can be found through the Qantas website or through British Airways. The Alaska Mileage Plan price is the same 55,000 miles for either carrier.

Earn miles through the Alaska Airlines Visa card sign-up bonus (typically 60,000 to 75,000 miles), through flying Alaska or partners, or by transferring from Marriott Bonvoy. If transferring from Marriott, allow 1 to 5 business days for the transfer to complete before your booking window closes.

Call Alaska Mileage Plan at 1-800-252-7522 and request a partner award booking on Cathay Pacific (or Qantas) Business Class. Provide your desired dates and routing. Ask about adding a free stopover in Hong Kong if routing through HKG. The agent will process the booking and deduct 55,000 miles plus taxes and fees (typically $50 to $150).

After booking through Alaska, manage your seat selection directly through the Cathay Pacific website or app using your booking reference. Select a window or aisle seat in the 1-2-1 configuration — every seat has direct aisle access, so there is no wrong choice. You can also pre-order meals and manage other preferences through Cathay's platform.

Let's make this concrete. You and your partner want to celebrate a milestone — a sabbatical, a paid-off mortgage, financial independence itself — with a trip to Sydney. Here's exactly how this redemption plays out.

The Route: Los Angeles (LAX) → Hong Kong (HKG) → Sydney (SYD), on Cathay Pacific Business Class, with a 3-night stopover in Hong Kong.

Cash Price: A quick search on Google Flights confirms what you suspected — this itinerary in business class retails for approximately $8,000 per person during the shoulder season. During the Australian summer or holiday periods, it climbs closer to $11,000–$12,000.

Your Cost: 55,000 Alaska Mileage Plan miles + approximately $85 in taxes and fees. Per person.

CPP Calculation: At $8,000 cash value, your 55,000 miles are worth 14.5 cents per point — more than seven times what you'd get redeeming Alaska miles for domestic economy. At $12,000, you're at 21.8 cents per point, which is among the highest CPP figures available anywhere in the U.S. loyalty ecosystem.

In Hong Kong, Cathay Pacific's The Pier Business Class Lounge awaits during your stopover travel. It's widely regarded as one of the finest airport lounges in the world — noodle bar, live cooking stations, a spa treatment center, and a wine selection that rivals dedicated restaurants.

After three days exploring Hong Kong, you reboard for the six-hour SYD leg, arriving in Sydney ready — genuinely ready, not depleted — to start your adventure.

Total cost for two: 110,000 Alaska miles + roughly $170 in fees. That's the FI mindset applied to travel: extraordinary experiences made nearly free through a system anyone can learn.

Alaska's booking window opens 331 days out. Cathay Pacific releases business class award space to partner programs in limited quantities, and the best dates disappear quickly. Set a calendar alert for 331 days before your target travel date and be ready to search — and call — that morning.

The single best technique for this redemption: run your search on ba.com before calling Alaska. BA's search engine is faster, more reliable for Cathay availability, and lets you visually scan a full month of dates. Identify two or three date options before you pick up the phone. This dramatically shortens your call time and reduces the chance of getting an agent who says "I'm not seeing anything."

Don't treat the Hong Kong stopover as a layover — treat it as a destination. Alaska's routing rules explicitly allow a free stopover on one-way awards. Two to four nights in Hong Kong costs you nothing extra in miles. Pair this with a cheap positioning flight or use it as an anchor for a broader Asia itinerary.

This is the most common and most painful mistake. Marriott-to-Alaska transfers are generally not reversible. If you transfer 165,000 Bonvoy points to Alaska and then discover no award space exists on your dates, you're stuck with miles you may not use optimally. Always confirm availability on ba.com before initiating any transfer.

Book two one-way redemptions rather than a round-trip. This gives you full flexibility on return routing — you might come back on Qantas through another city, or extend your trip without penalty.

Since there are no major flexible currency transfer paths into Alaska (no Chase, Amex, or Citi transfers), the Alaska Airlines Visa Signature from Bank of America is your most efficient earning vehicle. The welcome bonus alone can cover a significant portion of this redemption. Pair with everyday spending in categories that earn elevated miles.

If Cathay availability is closed on your dates, Qantas Business Class to Australia prices at the same 55,000 miles. Qantas' "The Business" product on their A380 Sydney routes is exceptional in its own right — and availability patterns differ from Cathay, so checking both genuinely doubles your options.

This redemption is purpose-built for the FI-minded couple or solo traveler who is willing to invest some effort in the booking process in exchange for an extraordinary, nearly free experience. If you've been dreaming about Australia and refuse to pay $8,000–$12,000 for a business class ticket — but you're also not willing to spend 20+ hours crammed in economy for a trip this significant — this is your answer.

Minimum requirements: You need 55,000 Alaska Mileage Plan miles per person. For two travelers, that's 110,000 miles. If you're building from zero through the Alaska Visa, factor in 6–12 months of earning runway before booking.

Within a broader FI travel strategy, this redemption pairs well with a Marriott Bonvoy credit card for point accumulation and an Alaska Visa for direct mile earning. It's a medium-complexity move with a very high ceiling on value.

This redemption earns a **moderate difficulty rating** — and that rating is honest. It's not complicated in concept, but it has two specific friction points that trip up even experienced travel rewards enthusiasts. **Challenge 1: Earning the Miles** Alaska Mileage Plan's isolation from major flexible currency programs (no Chase Ultimate Rewards, no Amex Membership Rewards, no Citi ThankYou transfers directly) means you can't simply funnel points you already have into Alaska. The primary path is the Alaska Airlines Visa (Bank of America) or a Marriott Bonvoy conversion at an unfavorable 3:1 ratio. Plan your earning strategy well in advance. **Tip:** Prioritize the Alaska Visa signup bonus as your foundation, then supplement with Marriott points if needed. **Challenge 2: The Phone Booking Requirement** You cannot book this online. The call-in process intimidates people who've only ever booked travel digitally. **Tip:** Do your homework on ba.com first, have your dates ready, and approach the call as an informed customer — not someone asking for help finding availability. Agents respond well to specific, prepared callers. **Challenge 3: Cathay Award Availability** Cathay Pacific releases partner award space selectively and often in small quantities. Availability rated 3/5. **Tip:** Search exactly at the 331-day booking window, keep Qantas as your backup at the same price point, and be flexible with travel dates by even one or two days — a Tuesday departure often has inventory when Saturday doesn't. The good news: once you've done this once, you'll understand the system deeply enough to replicate it. The ChooseFI community has members who've booked this exact route multiple times. The first time takes effort. After that, it's a process you know cold.

The fastest path is the Alaska Airlines Visa Signature card from Bank of America, which typically offers a 60,000 to 75,000-mile sign-up bonus. That alone nearly covers the 55,000 miles needed. You can also transfer Marriott Bonvoy points at 3:1 (165,000 Bonvoy points equals 55,000 Alaska miles) or earn miles through flying Alaska and its partners.

Yes. You would book two separate one-way awards at 55,000 miles each. You could fly Cathay Pacific one direction and Qantas the other, or mix carriers based on availability. Each one-way can include its own free stopover.

Cathay Pacific typically releases Business Class award space 90 to 330 days before departure. The sweet spot for finding availability is usually 90 to 120 days out, when airlines release unsold premium cabin seats. Check frequently, as availability can appear and disappear quickly.

Alaska allows one free stopover on one-way awards. On a routing from the US to Australia via Hong Kong, you can stop in Hong Kong for any number of days at no additional miles cost. Simply tell the agent when booking that you want a stopover in HKG. This effectively gives you two destinations for the price of one redemption.

The Alaska Mileage Plan redemption for Cathay Pacific or Qantas Business Class to Australia is one of the most extraordinary sweet spots in travel rewards. At 55,000 miles for a seat that costs $5,000 to $12,000 in cash — with zero fuel surcharges and a free stopover in Hong Kong — this redemption delivers 9 to 22 cents per point. It requires more planning and effort than a simple hotel booking, but the payoff is a genuine luxury travel experience that proves the asymmetric value the FI community builds its travel rewards strategy around.

#9032. Linehouse reimagines industrial aesthetics for Jen Hangzhou hotel in Kohn Pedersen Fox-designed building

Photography by Jonathan Leijonhufvud and Wen Studio

International studio Linehouse has completed the interiors of the Jen hotel in Hangzhou, China, which features details that nod to local craft and the area’s industrial heritage.

The hotel, which is owned by the Shangri-La Hotel Group, is located along Hangzhou’s Dongxin River in an urban setting and flanked by two former industrial factory compounds.

The 18-floor hotel building was designed by US architecture firm Kohn Pedersen Fox, using steel, grey brick and glass to reference the site’s industrial past.

The same design approach was extended into the interior by Linehouse, which focuses on showcasing local craft and nods to the industrial elements of the former factories.

“Jen Hangzhou is an urban hotel that celebrates its neighbourhood context – one that layers history, craft, culture and rich materiality into a new perspective on Hangzhou,” Linehouse said.

The studio used earth-toned marble, oak panelling and relaxed furniture in the ground-floor lobby to create a calm and warm atmosphere.

At the entrance, guests are greeted by a textured artwork by artist Elsa Jeandedieu that depicts an abstract version of the bridges and canal close to the hotel.

Patchwork patterns on the marble floor and on a bespoke rug in the lobby were informed by the street layout and tile patterns of the surrounding neighbourhood.

All the hospitality spaces, including a restaurant, a bar and function rooms are located on the sixth floor.

The long, linear OpenHouse restaurant is wrapped by full-height glazing that invites natural light inside.

A timber design feature spans the ceiling and was informed by the craft of sunmao, a traditional timber joinery technique. It is highlighted by a thin black metal frame that supports suspended lighting.

At the centre of the restaurant, a coffee bar splits the space into a dining area on one side and an all-day lounge on the other.

In the private dining room, the timber canopy has an angled design and is decorated with burnt red and yellow hues. In the rest of the OpenHouse restaurant, rooms feature teal tiles and handmade ceramic wall lighting.

The adjacent Koan Bar is a triple-height venue characterised by an undulating black metal staircase that takes guests to a terrace on the upper floor, with incorporated platforms where guests can socialise.

The sinuous staircase is carved between walls lined with concrete panels, another nod to the site’s industrial heritage.

Beneath it, curved booths in walnut timber and tan leather provide intimate seating spaces.

Three interconnected spaces on the sixth floor, enveloped by undulating timber walls, will be used for events and intimate social gatherings. Like in the lobby, bespoke carpets feature patterns abstracted from urban details in the neighbourhood.

The seventh floor is dedicated to wellness and comprises a gym, a yoga room, a spa, a pool and changing rooms, made from tactile materials with muted tones to create a calm environment.

At the gym, a lava stone wall has engravings that illustrate movement, while the yoga room features hand-chiseled timber panels.

A sloped skylit annex accommodates the swimming pool.

The 176 guest rooms were conceived as “urban retreats”. Here, Linehouse used a restrained palette of gun metal, oak datum, textured render and tan leather to underline the industrial aesthetic.

“The public areas explore traditional craft techniques such as sunmao timber joinery, clay tiling and bricks, natural patterns, textures and renders, whilst the guestrooms explore a refined industrial aesthetic,” Linehouse said.

“Red brick, concrete, metal and bold forms reference the surrounding industrial environment whilst handcrafted tiles, vintage timber, colours and metals with different patinas introduce warmth, richness and texture.”

The guest rooms have curved ceilings that create indirect lighting and add softness to the space, while the bathrooms are illuminated by glass-block walls.

Founded by Alex Mok and Briar Hickling in 2013, Linehouse is an architecture and interior practice with studios in Shanghai, Hong Kong and Auckland.

It has recently designed Ink Ink Market in Shanghai with a translucent sloping facade, as well as the interiors for Bangkok’s Central Park shopping centre with three dramatic atriums, which was shortlisted of Retail Interior (large) by this year’s Dezeen Awards.

Area: 12,850 sqm Client: Kerry Properties Operator: Shangri-La Design principal: Alex Mok Design team: Wang Jue, Jingru Tong, Yunbin Lou, Cherngyu Chen, Inez Low, Yeling Guo, Aiwen Shao, Mia Zhou, Norman Wang, Yuechen Wu Lighting: LPA Decorative lighting: Kris Lite, Van Collection, Yi Design, Yun Zhao Studio, Fine Lumens, Santa & Cole, Audo, Timothy Oulton, La Nuit Design consultant: EDGE Design Interior contractor: Terart Decoration Design & Engineering Co., Ltd, Shenzhen Lead management consultant: Wong & Ouyang (HK) Ltd. LDI & structural consultant: Zhejiang Province Institute of Architectural Design and Research MEP engineer consultant: Hangzhou MJP Mechanical & Electrical Design Consultant Ltd.

#9031. Milan’s New San Siro Stadium and the BIAU’s 12 Awarded Projects: This Week’s Review

This week started with World Cities Day, which this year, in line with World Architecture Day, was an occasion to spotlight deficient access to adequate housing, secure tenure, basic services, and affordable living conditions worldwide. Once again, we are faced with a call to approach architecture and urban design differently, making design a social tool rather than merely a market tool. Examples of sensible approaches can be seen in this week's announcements: waste-based materials, adaptive reuse of industrial heritage, and the recognition of the evolving nature of drawing. The controversial proposal to replace Milan's San Siro Stadium with a new design by Foster + Partners raises questions about notions of value and beauty in the contemporary world, while at ArchDaily, we invite students to imagine new forms of urban life through architecture. To reasonable conflicts, creative solutions. Finally, in this week's radar, we received news from the XIV Ibero-American Biennial of Architecture and Urbanism (BIAU), held this year in Brasília; a new curved timber-and-concrete building by OODA in Lisbon; and a masterplan by SOM for a brand-new city in Egypt.

Regenerating the City: Changing the Criteria We Build By

Urban designers are being asked to regenerate rather than simply expand, and that means revisiting the criteria used to build and rebuild cities. World Cities Day 2026, observed on October 31 under the theme "Regenerating the City: Adequate Housing for All," highlighted the United Nations' estimate that up to 3.4 billion people lack adequate housing and approached the challenge through housing, public space, mobility, and neighborhood livability. To improve the urban quality of life to contemporary standards, it's time to change the modern design guidelines that shaped many of our cities, including car-oriented planning. In London, Oxford Street opened its first traffic-free phase, almost a kilometer between Orchard Street and Great Portland Street, in a project led by landscape and urban design practice East that adds seating, planting, and places to meet and rest to a historic area long reserved for automobiles.

Projects to Look Forward To: Earth, Reuse, and the Value of the Already Built

Projects of international relevance were announced this week, each one proposing its own connection to heritage and pre-existing structures. In Sharjah, Taller de Arquitectura – Mauricio Rocha and Daniel Rosselló unveiled the Sharjah Design Centre, due in 2029, which incorporates rammed earth and sits within a research agenda on local and waste-based materials, placing material sustainability at the center of the project. In California, Herzog & de Meuron and EHDD will convert a mid-century warehouse into a museum for the Eames Institute of Infinite Curiosity, an adaptive reuse initiative that preserves the building's folded concrete roof and industrial imprint. In Milan, Foster + Partners and MANICA revealed the first images of their Generali Stadium, expected to replace San Siro, raising protests and questions. Why does our culture tend to see the new as intrinsically better? Where are we looking for beauty and value?

XIV BIAU Announces Winning Projects and Launches Its Program of Activities in Brasília

The XIV Bienal Iberoamericana de Arquitectura y Urbanismo (Ibero-American Biennial of Architecture and Urbanism, BIAU) opened in Brasília with the inauguration of its exhibition at SESI Lab and the announcement of this edition's winners. Under the theme "Cuidar la Vida" (Caring for Life), the jury recognized twelve projects, six in the Works category and six in Publications, along with five honorable mentions in Obras. The selected designs include a park in Brazil, a floating cinema in Perú, a rural development center in Ecuador, a theater in Chile, and social housing in Spain and Paraguay. Awarded publications explore themes such as the role of architecture in education, historical memory, urban transformation, and environmental challenges. All of the awarded works place care for people and territory at the center of architectural practice, addressing the integration of vegetation and water into built spaces, community life, and access to housing. The Biennial, promoted by Spain's Ministry of Housing and Urban Agenda (MIVAU), continues through November 6 with exhibitions, lectures, debates, and thematic tours across the city.

SOM Unveils Masterplan for a New Coastal City in Egypt

The first phase of Alam Al Roum, a new coastal city masterplan by Skidmore, Owings & Merrill (SOM) on Egypt's Mediterranean coast, is planned across approximately 4 million square meters, with delivery scheduled to begin in 2030. The initial development will include 2 kilometers of beachfront and promenade, open-sea-connected lagoons, residential and hospitality projects, a town-center marina, and retail and dining areas. The larger 20.6-million-square-meter masterplan envisions a year-round coastal destination organized around interconnected residential, mixed-use, hospitality, education, and business districts. Extending across 7.2 kilometers of coastline, the city is structured around seawater-connected lagoons, which extend the waterfront inland while contributing to stormwater management. Walking paths and trails connect shaded streets, gardens, promenades, and public spaces, complemented by cycling routes and planned transit connections. The masterplan also incorporates climate-responsive design, renewable energy generation, wetlands, stabilized dunes, and a living shoreline to address the site's environmental conditions and changing coastal dynamics.

#9030. Surrogacy Nearly Destroyed Our Marriage. It Also Brought Us Back

From the outside, our relationship looked the way it had for 24 years: solid.

After our first surrogacy experience ended in stillbirth, our friends were convinced we’d be fine because we were the “most together couple” they knew. I wasn’t so sure. For months, it had felt like my husband Ethan and I were two bodies fumbling to find each other in the dark. At home, our orbits rarely intersected. My eyes barely landed on Ethan. Once, he didn’t realize I was right behind him and he closed the door on me.

It felt like we were suspended in the quiet between the cracks and the crumble. We weathered life-altering challenges together in our 20s and 30s due to my whole-body symptoms from endometriosis, adenomyosis, early menopause, and a medical system that trivialized them all. My condition rattled our intimacy, upended my career, and made Ethan my caretaker. Being undiagnosed for decades also cost us my fertility, depleting my ovarian reserve and leading to miscarriage after miscarriage with IVF and IUIs.

Though we weren’t living the life we dreamed, and I felt guilty for the weight I foisted on Ethan, we managed to maintain the joie de vivre we’d had since we first met—until we turned to surrogacy.

Our decision to opt for an egg donor and a surrogate was an act of compromise. Though I’d always been ambivalent about motherhood, the idea of coparenting with Ethan had gradually filled me with tenderness and curiosity. But by then, after years of illness, I wanted a hysterectomy. Ethan still really wanted to be a dad. Neither of us wanted to jeopardize my wellness with more hormonal treatments and pregnancy losses, so we took what people called the “easy way out.” Though I was criticized by my doctors for giving up on my eggs and my uterus “too soon,” our decision to pursue surrogacy felt liberating—at first.

We thought finding a gestational surrogate would be the hardest part. Turns out, we were wrong. Instead, we were totally unprepared for the ways surrogacy was going to change our marriage.

Our first surrogacy experience was the kind we now caution other intended parents against. We entrusted an agency with our fate and our funds, putting them in charge of introducing us to a surrogate and acting as the intermediary who would reimburse her for pregnancy-related expenses on our behalf. At the time, we were unaware of their proven fraudulent history.

Not only were Ethan and I new to surrogacy, but we also felt vulnerable—maybe even desperate. We were privileged to have found someone who wanted to do this for us, and we wanted to be generous and grateful. You also don’t have much control when your baby is in someone else’s womb and your funds are in a corporation’s bank account. So we ignored the red flags we noticed with the agency’s inflated reimbursements and our surrogate’s jarring mood fluctuations.

If we’d shared our worries with each other early on, we may have had a chance to course-correct. At least I wouldn’t have felt so alone carrying this angst in my bones. At one of our second-trimester ultrasounds, I resented Ethan for being his jovial self while he talked to our active baby boy through the screen as I stood hunched against the wall, struggling to feel present. It wasn’t just that the pregnancy felt unbearably abstract for me as a mother who didn’t contribute her genes or her womb; I was also increasingly skeptical of the agency and walking on eggshells with our surrogate, who’d keep us at arm’s length one week and accuse us of not being supportive enough the next. I’d never gotten this far in a pregnancy and it should have been a happy time. Instead, I bottled up my distress and couldn’t breathe from the weight of it.

During our first surrogacy experience, Ethan let me bear the brunt of the conversations with our surrogate. He thought he had a supportive role, but his not being in the foreground put extra weight on my shoulders and took my time, energy, and headspace while sparing him. I was also the one who handled all the legal and financial paperwork, and the communication with the agency. Ethan was grateful and proud of me for managing what he considered more in my wheelhouse than his, but I felt paralyzing stress and resentment having to tackle these hard tasks on my own at such a vulnerable time.

Our breaking point was brought on by our different ways of grieving. While I naturally tend to dig deep into painful topics and emotions to make sense of them, Ethan prefers to compartmentalize. At the hospital after the delivery, Ethan preferred to leave the room when I stayed to spend a few minutes with our stillborn. I wanted the loss to feel more tangible, while he wanted to hold onto the joy from other memories, like when we saw him on ultrasounds. Neither of us was wrong, but we were disconnected.

The months that followed were agony because none of the doctors would counsel us on why our baby had died simply because I wasn’t the pregnant patient, as though we weren’t his parents and didn’t have the right to know. I spiraled into depression and was furious every time Ethan would tell his parents that we were fine. He didn’t want to burden them, but I didn’t want to mask our reality for the sake of others’ comfort. For 24 years—through long distance, sickness, and grief—we’d been the “strong couple” who never argued. Now, in the complexity of surrogacy, we kept snapping at each other because Ethan needed a semblance of normalcy and I needed to dwell in darkness.

So how do you come back to each other when who you were didn’t survive? Over nearly a year, thanks to our self-awareness, deep respect for one another, and therapy (which Ethan hated attending but did when required), we made three tiny shifts that saved our marriage.

When we met our second surrogate through a more ethical, transparent, and supportive agency that did not demand funds in trust, Ethan and I formed a true trio with her. It helped that she considered us a team and wanted our involvement in appointments, decisions, and her daily life. She’d use the word “together” so often that it initially triggered us; it felt so foreign to us after our first surrogacy journey, and we couldn’t tell which of the two experiences was the anomaly. Ethan made it a priority to participate in our conversations and replied to our group texts if I couldn’t. We all shared freely—our fears, dreams, victories, recipes, and silly inside jokes—and the three of us built an intimacy I never expected. When it was just the two of us, our surrogate was never far from our thoughts, as if our marriage had expanded to include her.

Ethan also started to help me with the challenging legal and financial tasks. He kept up with emails he was CC’ed on during the day and sat with me if we had paperwork to tackle, his hand on my back if I got overwhelmed.

When we lost our baby with our second surrogate at the end of the first trimester, we grieved as a unit. Our trio sat intertwined, our hands piled on my lap. At home, Ethan was more receptive to my needs on my bad days. Just watching him witness me in those moments, even if all he did was listen and sigh, brought us closer together. I was more understanding when he clung to his social activities to blow off steam. Ethan was more honest with family and friends about our emotional and financial distress. He agreed to ask for help and for a loan to help us get back on our feet after two surrogacy journeys and thirteen years of fertility and ongoing health expenses.

We decided not to talk about surrogacy on weekends or right before bed to give our nervous systems a chance to unwind. Dark humor helped us grieve: We’d sometimes whisper jaded comments to each other when triggered. When we imagine something creative we would have done with our kid, we say, “File it under never!” During the holidays, Ethan toasted me with, “Cheers to not losing a child this Christmas!” Holding space for our contrasting ways of grieving and meeting in the middle helped dissolve the resentment and tension between us.

Fertility treatments and surrogacy can become all-consuming for a couple, especially after decades of illness and loss. Being diagnosed with post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) after our first surrogacy experience further shook my identity. We started making a conscious effort to remember what was special about our life and our love before all this. We are more than what we carry and what we’ve lost.

Besides carving out periods of play, nature, and grief-free talk, we also pushed ourselves to keep money aside for leisure and travel—not just for our living expenses and surrogacy costs—so we can look forward to something in our calendar and savor new experiences together.

We found, though, that the least daunting way of rebuilding our future is to simply take care of our present. Often, all we can handle is the next half-hour: where to take a walk, what to make for supper, how to support each other right then. I worked hard to keep my eyes focused on Ethan until it became natural again. Even now, as we grapple with whether and how to continue with our surrogacy journey, when we start acting like passing ships because of our full heads and aching hearts, we drop everything, hug, touch.

I never expected our strong marriage to be impacted by the most tender gift we gave each other: the chance to grow our family through surrogacy. We’d naively thought what awaited us would be easier than the road that led there. Our experiences with surrogacy have changed how we show up for each other, both in joy and in grief.

I can’t say for certain that our marriage is now strong enough to survive anything that lies ahead. What I know is this: We’ve built what we’ll need to recalibrate our direction to find each other in the dark.

#9029. Studio Shea designs South Carolina library as "community living room"

Photography by Keith Isaacs (unless stated otherwise)

Brooklyn-based practice Studio Shea has completed a metal-clad library with a central atrium that draws on the civic and industrial context of its site in South Carolina, USA.

Clinton Public Library serves a railroad junction town of less than 8,000 residents.

The 11,000-square-foot (1,021-square metre) library translates the vernacular porch feature as well as the town’s agricultural and textile manufacturing heritage into a contemporary public building, Justin Shea, founder of Studio Shea, told Dezeen.

“At its core, the project was conceived as a welcoming community living room,” Shea said.

Set on 1.25 acres, the building’s scale and massing respond to its surrounding residential context in view of the town’s downtown corridor.

“The deep roof overhang creates a shaded front porch that recalls the familiar social role of the porch as a place for gathering,” Shea said, explaining that the low-pitched roofs and striated standing-seam metal cladding are a subtle nod to the area’s material character.

“Together, these elements give the library a contemporary identity while maintaining a clear connection to the character and history of Clinton.”

Inside, the library centres around a daylit atrium that is both the social and organisational heart of the program spaces and collections.

From the entrance, library patrons can see through the atrium to the collections, study areas, activity spaces and reading garden in a clear, easy-to-navigate scheme.

“Particular attention was given to the quality of natural light,” said Shea.

“A continuous clerestory draws soft, even daylight deep into the building, activating the interior throughout the day. At night, the illuminated atrium reverses that relationship, allowing the library to glow outward as a beacon for the community.”

The plan was designed for adaptability and flexibility, with the makerspace, children’s room, and meeting areas expanding into the center for larger workshops and the community room connecting with the lobby, service spaces and exterior plaza for after-hours events.

Inside, pops of colour, monochromatic spaces and varied textures create a playful environment suited to a broad range of ages and activities, while generous glazing contributes to the sense of openness.

A key element of the design is a community bench along the building’s exterior – designed by Studio Shea and fabricated with oak trees from the site by Piedmont Technical College – that ties into the lobby bench, circulation desk and collection shelving.

“What might otherwise have been an incidental site resource became a tangible expression of local participation and investment,” Shea explained.

“Public architecture can create a stronger sense of ownership when the community is given opportunities to participate in its creation,” he continued.

“A civic building does not need to be monumental to be significant; it can achieve meaning through being welcoming, useful, adaptable and genuinely connected to the people and place it serves.”

Other public buildings recently completed in South Carolina include a county administration building with “crisp edges” by Foster + Partners, the International African American Museum that floats above water by Pei Cobb Freed & Partners and Moody Nolan and a seaside restaurant designed for nostalgia by SDCO and Basic Projects.

Text description provided by the architects. House with Rope and Ladder, located in a small village on the southeast coast of Sweden, is a project in two parts: a traditional rendered masonry volume with a gable roof, adhering to the rather strict regulations of the site, and an enclosed circular garden, attached tangentially to the middle of the house.

#9026. Sharjah Architecture Triennial 2026 Announces Opening Programme Featuring Performances, Films, and Conference

The Sharjah Architecture Triennial (SAT) has announced the opening programme of its third edition, Architecture Otherwise: Building Civic Infrastructure for Collective Futures. Curated by writer and anthropologist Vyjayanthi Rao, with Associate Curator Tau Tavengwa, the Triennial will take place from November 14, 2026, to April 14, 2027, with its six-day opening programme running from November 14 to 19. Co-curated by Rao and Sharmeen Inayat, SAT's Research and Civic Engagement Curator, the programme brings together participatory projects, live performances, film screenings, lectures, and discussions across the Emirate of Sharjah, culminating in a two-day international conference on November 18 and 19.

The Sharjah Architecture Triennial (SAT) has announced the opening programme of its third edition, Architecture Otherwise: Building Civic Infrastructure for Collective Futures. Curated by writer and anthropologist Vyjayanthi Rao, with Associate Curator Tau Tavengwa, the Triennial will take place from November 14, 2026, to April 14, 2027, with its six-day opening programme running from November 14 to 19. Co-curated by Rao and Sharmeen Inayat, SAT's Research and Civic Engagement Curator, the programme brings together participatory projects, live performances, film screenings, lectures, and discussions across the Emirate of Sharjah, culminating in a two-day international conference on November 18 and 19.

The third edition brings together 35 participants whose multidisciplinary practices examine architecture through the relationships, knowledge, and forms of exchange that shape collective life. Events will take place across several locations, including Al Qasimiyah School, Al Jubail Vegetable Market, Al Madam Buried Village, and the Sharjah Museum of Islamic Civilization. Throughout the opening week, participant-led tours and live interventions will engage visitors with the Triennial's installations and research, including Tumblespace (or What Binds Us?) by Aslıhan Demirtaş, Ali Cindoruk, and Dilşad Aladağ. The nomadic structure explores connections between people, movement, and place through temporary spaces for gathering and exchange. Badriyah Alsalem will also present The Houses of the Moon and Names of the Sun, performance lectures drawing on observation, poetry, and cultural astronomy to examine relationships between landscape, time, and the sky.

The programme will also include performances exploring the relationship between sound, movement, and spatial experience. Pakistani-American singer Ali Sethi will present BORROWED TIME: trails and tentacles in popular music, while choreographer Omar Rajeh's Origami Bodies will be presented in dialogue with Ziad Jamaleddine's SAT project Lalla Alwyia, Khalwa. The collaboration brings together movement informed by maqam, a practice of instantaneous composition, and a reinterpretation of the khalwa, a secluded space traditionally associated with Sufi retreat and meditation.

Film screenings will examine urban development, housing, and the social histories embedded within city infrastructure. The Tower: A Concrete Utopia, by Filip De Boeck and Sammy Baloji, considers independent approaches to urban space in Kinshasa, while Cassim Shepard's Housing Agency: Incremental Mumbai explores how informal settlement practices have influenced alternative housing approaches in India. Ignacio Gatica's Sanhattan examines Santiago's financial district and its relationship to New York, and Ruchir Joshi's Memories of Milk City addresses memory and displacement in Ahmedabad.

Conversations and roundtables will bring architects, artists, researchers, and cultural practitioners into dialogue with SAT03 participants and curators. The opening conversation, Building Civic Muscles, will examine how everyday practices, identities, economies, and social relations shape the built environment. Edgar Pieterse, Mabel O. Wilson, and Paola Antonelli will join Rao and Tavengwa for the discussion. Other sessions include The Action is the Form, moderated by Sharmeen Inayat, and The Trouble with Images, featuring filmmaker Rania Stephan and artist Amarnath Praful, moderated by Thomas Keenan. Additional roundtables will address urban transformation in the Gulf, the relationship between cities and time, and sound as a spatial practice, including a session featuring Yousef and Elias Anastas of Radio Alhara.
