The opening week will conclude with the two-day conference Area Studies, Global Studies and Urban Studies: History, Politics and the Epistemology of Locality, organised in collaboration with Global Studies University and hosted at Africa Hall. Bringing together international scholars, architects, artists, and researchers, the conference will examine how knowledge about cities and regions is produced and how local histories and experiences challenge dominant narratives of urban development. Its panels will address ecological and temporal negotiations in architecture, everyday urban planning, and the institutions and collective practices that emerge following rupture and displacement. Participants include Rachaporn Choochuey, Soumini Raja, Mona El Mousfy, Hessa Al Nuaimi, Catalina Ortiz, Neha Vora, Dubravka Sekulić, Emily Jacir, Filip de Boeck, Ibrahim Nehme, and Camila Palomino.

#9025. What AI Reveals About Architecture That Was Never Built

Some architectural projects only survive as drawings, competition entries, or models in archives. Others were built, but not as first imagined, and the completed building gradually replaced the original proposal in collective memory. Christopher Wren's St. Paul's Cathedral is familiar to many, but less well known is his Warrant Design, the spire-topped proposal approved in 1675 that he subsequently reworked as construction progressed. London was also once offered a very different monument: Thomas Willson's vast pyramid-shaped necropolis for Primrose Hill, designed to accommodate millions of burials and dominate the city's skyline.

Some architectural projects only survive as drawings, competition entries, or models in archives. Others were built, but not as first imagined, and the completed building gradually replaced the original proposal in collective memory. Christopher Wren's St. Paul's Cathedral is familiar to many, but less well known is his Warrant Design, the spire-topped proposal approved in 1675 that he subsequently reworked as construction progressed. London was also once offered a very different monument: Thomas Willson's vast pyramid-shaped necropolis for Primrose Hill, designed to accommodate millions of burials and dominate the city's skyline.

These projects have outlived the circumstances that prevented their realization, whether financial, political, or technical. Some addressed practical needs through extraordinary forms; others explored how infrastructure, buildings, and cities could support new ways of living. New visualization technologies offer ways to revisit these works and examine ideas that, in some cases, anticipated the scale and complexity of contemporary megaprojects. A series being developed by Gendo explores this possibility through historical proposals that were never built or underwent significant changes before completion. Using archival drawings, models, and descriptions as starting points, it considers how generative tools might bring these ideas into view for contemporary audiences, while making clear where documentation ends and interpretation begins.

Among the earlier proposals is Charles-François Ribart de Chamoust's colossal triumphal elephant for the Champs-Élysées, conceived in 1758 with elaborate interiors, including a dining room with trees and a stream. A later elephant monument proposed under Napoleon for the Place de la Bastille reached the stage of a full-scale plaster model, which remained on the site for decades. Claude-Nicolas Ledoux's work similarly extended beyond his built tollhouses for Paris to more unusual proposals, including classical structures on boats intended to collect tolls from river traders. In his cenotaph for Isaac Newton, Étienne-Louis Boullée imagined a monumental sphere whose interior would evoke the night sky.

In his cenotaph for Isaac Newton, Étienne-Louis Boullée imagined a monumental sphere whose interior would evoke the night sky.

Early twentieth-century proposals explored the possibilities of new materials, infrastructure, and urban organization. Antonio Sant'Elia's Città Nuova imagined a layered city of elevators, bridges, and power stations, with a visual language that invites comparison with the later worlds of Metropolis and Blade Runner. Mies van der Rohe's Friedrichstraße skyscraper explored the architectural potential of a glass envelope, while Erich Mendelsohn's sketches and Hermann Finsterlin's proposals pursued expressive, almost biological forms.

Mies van der Rohe's Friedrichstraße skyscraper explored the architectural potential of a glass envelope, while Erich Mendelsohn's sketches and Hermann Finsterlin's proposals pursued expressive, almost biological forms.

Other projects challenged architectural conventions more directly. Adolf Loos, known for his criticism of ornament, entered the Chicago Tribune competition with a skyscraper shaped like a giant Doric column. The Hotel Attraction, a soaring tower proposed for Lower Manhattan and attributed to Antoni Gaudí, introduces a different question: how to interpret a project whose authorship and surviving drawings remain subjects of debate.

Postwar proposals expanded these ambitions to entire urban systems. Arata Isozaki's Clusters in the Air organized spaces around tree-like structural cores above Tokyo. Ron Herron's Walking City for Archigram imagined mobile structures crossing landscapes on telescopic legs. Rem Koolhaas's Bangkok Hyperbuilding proposed concentrating an entire urban environment within a single structure. Some of these projects were intended to be built on specific sites and others used drawings and models to explore ideas about architecture and urban life without aiming for construction.

Architectural visualization combines technical skill with decisions about composition, materials, lighting, context, and occupation. A photorealistic image can make a proposal immediately legible to viewers unfamiliar with architectural drawings. Producing such images has traditionally required considerable time and specialized expertise.

Architectural visualization combines technical skill with decisions about composition, materials, lighting, context, and occupation. A photorealistic image can make a proposal immediately legible to viewers unfamiliar with architectural drawings. Producing such images has traditionally required considerable time and specialized expertise.

The choice of medium also affects what an image communicates. A watercolor can suggest atmosphere while leaving details unresolved. A section can explain spatial relationships without describing every surface. Photorealism gives those surfaces and details greater apparent certainty, which can be useful when presenting a developed proposal but misleading when decisions are still provisional.

Historical architects worked with the representational tools available to them. Their drawings and models could communicate powerful visions, yet translating those visions for patrons, committees, or the public remained a challenge. The ability to make an unfamiliar idea understandable can influence whether it gains support, alongside questions of cost, feasibility, and political will.

Historical architects worked with the representational tools available to them. Their drawings and models could communicate powerful visions, yet translating those visions for patrons, committees, or the public remained a challenge. The ability to make an unfamiliar idea understandable can influence whether it gains support, alongside questions of cost, feasibility, and political will.

Generative visualization tools allow architects to turn an initial concept into an image more quickly and test different materials, lighting conditions, and viewpoints. Architects still need to decide what the image should communicate and which details to include. When revisiting historical projects, some of those details may be missing from the original drawings and choosing a facade material or placing people around a building can make its appearance and scale easier to understand, but these additions reflect decisions made today.

The Gendo series distinguishes between three approaches: evidence-based visualization, grounded interpretation, and open-ended provocation. Each image is intended to be labeled according to its relationship with the original documentation.

The Gendo series distinguishes between three approaches: evidence-based visualization, grounded interpretation, and open-ended provocation. Each image is intended to be labeled according to its relationship with the original documentation.

At the evidence-based end, the proposed visualization of Willson's pyramid uses survey data and defined camera positions to place the structure within aerial views of Primrose Hill and the wider London skyline. Drawing on methods used for verified views in planning applications, the exercise aims to test technical accuracy as well as visual persuasion. Mies's Friedrichstraße tower receives similar treatment within its Berlin site, while Wren's Warrant Design will be shown alongside the cathedral that was built, allowing direct comparison.

The rigor of these images depends on the underlying geometry, site information, and production process. Grounded interpretation allows more room for decisions where the historical record is incomplete. Original drawings, descriptions, and photographs of models guide the work, while lighting, materials, and surroundings give the proposals a more tangible presence. The Hotel Attraction in Lower Manhattan, Boullée's cenotaph on a plausible French site, and Isozaki's clusters reconstructed from photographs of his models fall within this approach.

Open-ended provocation deliberately moves further from literal reconstruction. Finsterlin's and Mendelsohn's expressive forms can become starting points for experiments that follow the spirit of their work, potentially in dialogue with the visual worlds of H. R. Giger or M. C. Escher. Loos's column-shaped tower invites another kind of response: covering it in graffiti and tattoos would revisit the architect's own associations between ornament and bodily decoration. None of these images constitutes a definitive completion of another architect's work. Their labels help explain how much rests on historical evidence and how much comes from contemporary imagination.

The series also places historical proposals in dialogue with later projects and visual cultures. Boullée's cenotaph, for example, can be considered alongside the LED-covered Sphere proposed for Stratford in London, a counterpart to the venue in Las Vegas that was refused planning permission in 2023. Although radically different in purpose, the two spherical monuments invite a comparison of what different periods choose to monumentalize: scientific understanding and the cosmos in one case, entertainment in the other.

#9023. Fragile lighting collection by Marset among 15 new products on Dezeen Showroom

A lighting range comprising repeatable spherical and pyramidal forms made from delicate glass is among recent products published on our furniture directory.

Fragile lighting collection by Jaume Ramírez for Marset

A simple table lamp, created by designer Jaume Ramírez for Marset, comprising a round base and pointed shade, has been spun out into a larger lighting range using the same visual language.

Fragile is now a full collection spanning table, wall and pendant lights of varying scales, providing elegant lighting solutions for spaces of all sizes.

Other products featured on Dezeen Showroom recently include playful task chairs with pop-coloured bases and a modular furnishing system designed to zone open-plan offices.

Read on to find out about some of our latest products:

Flora armchair by Andreas Engesvik for Fogia

This dining chair is the result of a three-way collaboration between Swedish brand Fogia, designer Andreas Engesvik and Michelin three-star chef Esben Holmboe Bang, who works out of Oslo restaurant Maaemo.

Flora‘s cantilevered arms, padded backrest, thickly upholstered seat and slender frame aim to make users as comfortable as possible, providing the stamina for hours of seated conversation and dining.

Flora armchair by Andreas Engesvik for Fogia

Dining, side and coffee tables comprise this collection by Philippine design brand Reforma and designers Eri and Mikka Mangaran.

Arcos aims to soften the sharp lines and corners commonly found in table design, an effect furthered by solid oak or walnut materiality, which has a natural finish.

Japanese office brand Kokuyo has created an ergonomic chair that features a pioneering integrated self-adjusting mechanism as well as a cocooning backrest made from taut mesh.

Named ingCloud, the chair was designed to facilitate easy movement rather than perfect, rigid posture across the course of a working day.

Lighting brand Neoz has released a compact, statuesque table lamp that’s cordless design facilitates uncluttered tablescapes.

Cooee 1c comprises a dome-shaped shade and all-metal body, which casts atmospheric pools of light on dining tables.

Kili tables by Mario Ferrarini for Lapalma

Designer Mario Ferrarini has released a collection of tables that are informed by the movement of turning.

Kili tables were made for Italian brand Lapalma and come in various finishes and colourway options.

Estonian brand Silen has released a new line of office booths, creating controlled environments for one-to-one meetings as well as calls and focused solo work.

Space Gen 2 office pods boast various performance- and environmental-related credentials, including a frame made from 50 per cent recycled aluminium and a “floating roof” for enhanced airflow capabilities.

HÅG Minu by Andreas Engesvik and Jannicke Grung for Flokk

Designers Andreas Engesvik and Jannicke Grung of eponymous studio Grung Engesvik have created this compact and casual task chair for Flokk.

HÅG Minu comes in six base colour options and a variety of upholstery materials, and was created to be straightforward to disassemble and repair as needed in order to extend its lifespan.

HUB modular system by Francesco Rota for Lapalma

Designer Francesco Rota and Italian furniture brand Lapalma have worked together to release this modular seating system that has a fully upholstered form supported by a slimline frame.

The HUB modular system is made up of various module types that come together to form flowing, curvilinear seating solutions that snake through large-scale interiors.

British furniture brand Boss Design has created a series of office pods named Mews that span small, medium and large scales and can host solo individuals up to large groups.

The pods can be used in clusters to facilitate meetings, focused work or calls in one location, or can be dotted around to spread functionality through spaces.

The Dolce and Vita tile range by Spanish brand Roca is cement-informed and flecked with chip-like inclusions, respectively.

Both styles come in either cool-toned grey or warm-toned beige variations, making them suitable for a range of interior schemes.

German brand Visplay has developed a grid-structured furniture system named Spatio Office that provides structure and zoning in offices that are open-plan or in the process of evolving.

The structures are formed of metal frames fitted with a choice of solid walls, mesh and curtains, and have the capacity to be accessorised with additional planters, storage and pinboards for added functionality and personalisation.

Victoria Aged Brass cordless table lamp by Neoz

A compact, burnished brass body and a choice of fabric shades characterise this small but distinguished table lamp by lighting brand Neoz.

The Victoria Aged Brass cordless table lamp is intended for use on tables in hospitality environments, where its cordless nature prevents excess tabletop clutter.

Turkish brand Parla worked with design studio Goodrich on this fully upholstered armchair bisected at each corner with wedge-like slivers of timber.

The Hew armchair comes in various upholstery options and colourways for the legs, creating further customisation options for an already distinctive seat.

Visplay’s Qubo Office system aims to make use of blank walls or create new partitions that can be accessorised with functional add-ons.

Open metal shelving has a minimalist appeal when left bare, or can become a bank of planters, storage units and lockers.

#9022. Ersatzneubau Winkel / Kollektiv.w AG

Text description provided by the architects. A House in the Green – Nestled between residential buildings and mature trees stood a small former production hall. Originally, it was to be preserved and extended with a senior-friendly apartment, but structural assessments revealed that this would only be possible with extensive interventions. Due to these challenges and the limited space, a replacement building was planned, with a floor plan based on the former hall.
